items.title: Dutch & Austrian Embassies Damaged In Russian Drone Strikes On Ukrainian Capital
items.content_text:
Dutch & Austrian Embassies Damaged In Russian Drone Strikes On Ukrainian Capital

The Dutch Embassy in Ukraine's capital has suffered damage after a Russian drone struck a building just behind it. The embassy has sustained minor damage, with no diplomats or staff having been hurt in the attack, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said.

Berendsen wrote on X, "This afternoon, a projectile struck behind the Dutch embassy in Kyiv. Fortunately, our colleagues are unharmed, though there is some minor damage to the building. We are investigating exactly what happened. Our priority now is the well-being of our staff." The Austrian Embassy was also reportedly hit in the widespread attack. At least one person was killed in the broad attacks on the capital. Some initial images that emerged in the aftermath:

The Dutch government within hours after the Thursday afternoon strike summoned the Russian ambassador in ​the Netherlands to demand answers.

This conversation is unlikely to go well, and Russia's representative is unlikly to be very apologetic. Instead, the Kremlin has been outraged that drones from Dutch weapons startup Destinus were used to attack and significantly damage the Crimean Bridge on Tuesday.

Even Zelensky had confirmed that the company's 'Ruta' drone-missiles had been used, stating it quite openly in a social media post Tuesday.

Russia's Embassy in Amsterdam has warned Thursday that this act risks making the The Netherlands a direct party to the Ukraine war. It published a message and warning, saying:

Against this backdrop, it is becoming increasingly difficult to regard the Netherlands as a mere bystander. Through its actions, The Hague is consistently deepening its involvement in the conflict, contributing to its prolongation and further escalation. As the Russian leadership has repeatedly emphasised, it is evident that every effort is being made in Europe to undermine a long-term peaceful settlement of the Ukrainian conflict. At the same time, it should be clearly understood that, regardless of any obstacles, our country will achieve all the stated objectives of the special military operation.

So naturally there's going to be a high degree of suspicion in Europe that Moscow intentially targeted the Dutch Embassy, given it is now at the center of the Kremlin's ratcheting rhetoric and threats.

Ukraine's Minister of Foreign Affairs is meanwhile condemning what he calls 'terrorist strikes' on the capital, with the Ukrainians also now suggesting the attacks on the embassies were intentional.

Just the day prior, Dutch arms manufacturer Destinus had stepped out of the shadows and openly proclaimed its role in the earlier Crimean Bridge attack, confirming that seven of its RUTA drone-missiles destroyed part of the crossing.

"We are proud to support the Ukrainian defence forces in their fight to defend Ukraine and Europe," the Hengelo and Valkenburg-based company announced in a LinkedIn post. It marked the first time that Destinus has ever publicly claimed that its weapons were behind attack operations by Ukraine.

The Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs also reportedly suffered damage from drone debris during the assault.

The accusations from NATO-land have been pouring in....

Yesterday Moscow directly warned The Netherlands, and today the Dutch Embassy suffers damage... coincidence?

Tyler Durden Thu, 11/19/2026 - 13:50

items.title: Anthropic Opens 34% Above IPO Price, Market Cap Tops $2 Trillion
items.content_text:
Anthropic Opens 34% Above IPO Price, Market Cap Tops $2 Trillion

Summary:

  • ANT has opened for trading at $111.50, 34% above the IPO Price
  • Anthropic IPO Allocates Nothing to Most Institutional Orders
  • Anthropic-Linked Perpetual Futs On Hyperliquid $104
  • Anthropic IPO Prices At $83, Raises A Record $107 Billion

Anthropic Opens At $111.50

CEO Dario Amodei just helped ring the opening bell at the Nasdaq. 

Anthropic shares just opened (just before midday) at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price of $83, trading under the symbol "ANT". 

That opening price pushes the not-yet-six-year-old company's market capitalization above $2 trillion.

Seeing some selling pressure out of the gate...

The broad market is extending losses after the ANT open...

Low Institutional Offering, Stocks Sink

Anthropic's IPO is said to have given nothing to most institutional buyers. 

We see two possibilities for why:

  • Either the deal was going so well that the bookrunners were able to fill retail buyers and cut the institutional back so much that they’ll guarantee a pop on the shares and outperformance as the company joins indexes and investors are forced to buy it.
  • Or they couldn’t find institutional investors who were willing to pay $83 a share so they crammed it into retail bidders who were less discriminating on price. 

For now, the early squeeze in stocks has faded very rapidly. As the indicative price for Anthropic's IPO open increases (latest around $105 from $83 IPO), so the US Majors have tumbled since the US cash market opened...

...and SPX has broken back below its 200DMA...

ANT IPO Countdown; Here's Where Gray Market Trades 

Anthropic's massive market debut this morning is shaping up as one of the most critical tests for the AI trade after its oversubscribed IPO and private placement were upsized to $107.3 billion, exceeding SpaceX's fundraising record set in early summer.

The Claude chatbot developer priced its shares at $83, above the $70 to $78 range in its prospectus, implying a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion.

Trading under the ticker "ANT" on the Nasdaq Global Select Market could begin around 10 a.m. ET, according to Nasdaq. However, matching the substantial order book could push the first trade into late morning or early afternoon.

Ahead of the debut, Anthropic-linked perpetual futures on crypto platform Hyperliquid have traded at premiums of roughly 20% to 26% to the IPO price, with contracts around $104.20.

"A strong debut could restore confidence in AI valuations," Betashares analyst Hugh Lam said, adding that the IPO is being watched as a "verdict on the wider AI trade."

The big question today is whether investors will chase Anthropic for fear of missing out (FOMO) on the AI trade of the year, or balk at a valuation of roughly 11x projected next-year revenue, a hefty premium. At $1.5 trillion, how much of the AI revolution is already baked in for now?

Bloomberg Opinion's Nir Kaissar writes:

That is, unless Anthropic hoards all the profits. Don't count on it. 

The problem with outsized profits is that they attract competition, which is arguably Anthropic's biggest vulnerability. It wasn’t that long ago that OpenAI's ChatGPT was the only chatbot anyone had heard of. 

Anthropic's Claude has made inroads because large language models have shallow moats: They're relatively easy to replicate, and brand loyalty is limited. Just ask Dario Amodei, who left OpenAI, where he helped lead research on GPT-2 and GPT-3 before founding Anthropic in 2021. 

What happened to OpenAI could easily happen to Anthropic. The proliferation of open models is a preview of their coming ubiquity. Anthropic will soon have numerous competitors worldwide, including in China.

Look at the fight Chinese electric-car manufacturers are giving Tesla Inc. — a business at least as complicated as developing LLMs.

With Nvidia's earnings in the rearview mirror, Anthropic's IPO in just a matter of hours, and Friday's derivatives expiration set to reshuffle positioning, Wall Street will head into Thanksgiving holiday week in a continued test: Will the biggest IPO in history give the AI trade a revival, or lead to an extended downturn? 

Anthropic IPO Prices At $83, Raises A Record $107 Billion... With Its Own Chip Suppliers Holding Up The Floor

Update: the revised IPO terms were just published by Anthropic, and instead of the 825 million shares offered previously, the new offering is 980 million shares, a 19% increase in the offering size. 

Today Anthropic, PBC priced its initial public offering of its Class A common stock at $83.00 per share. The offering consists of 980,000,000 shares of Class A common stock, 956,351,354 of which are being sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 of which are being sold by certain selling stockholders. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders.

The shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19, 2026 under the symbol “ANT.” The offering is expected to close on November 20, 2026, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions. In addition, Anthropic has granted the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional 147,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock.

And so it's official: Anthropic is about to be a $1.1 trillion company... or $1.5 trillion fully-diluted company depending - as we noted last week - on who's counting.

After a week in which the same "above the range" headline hit the tape three days in a row, the Claude maker priced its IPO at $83 a share on Wednesday, $5 above the top of the $70-$78 marketed range, and upsized the deal... and as of 6:40pm we learned by how much: from 825 million to 980 million. 

That means the IPO raises at least $81.3 billion and, with the $26 billion vendor placement, more than $107 billion in total, 43% more than SpaceX's $75 billion base deal in June (or $86.2 billion including the greenshoe); about 4.2x Saudi Aramco, and more than SK Hynix, Aramco, Alibaba and SoftBank combined. The greenshoe would add another $12.2BN, for about $119.5BN!

Shares start trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, with some speculating that the price was set so that the customary post-IPO 20% pop pushes the stock above $100. If doesn't, or if it closes red... watch out. 

Just don't call it a surprise.

To put the size in context, as Howard Marks pointed out last week, there's only so much new capital available in a given year: a typical year of US IPOs raises less than $50 billion. Anthropic just raised double that in one night.

The Number(s)

At $83, using the same share bridge we laid out when the range was filed: about 13.20 billion shares outstanding after the deal give an actual market cap of roughly $1.1 trillion, the number an index provider will use, up from $1.08 trillion before the upsizing. Add the 1.77 billion employee options (average strike: $2.91), the 1.07 billion unvested RSUs and the 2.05 billion shares reserved for grants nobody has received yet, and you get the $1.5 trillion fully diluted figure that will lead every headline. 

Either way, it's a long way from the "$2 trillion or more" that was being whispered in early October: 25% below on a fully diluted basis, 45% below on shares outstanding. It's also 41% above the $58.90 per share (post-split) that Series H buyers paid in May at a $965 billion post-money, and right around the "$1.5 trillion or more" the FT said bankers were pushing for. 

It's not just the company selling shares: insiders will become instantly rich too - each of the seven co-founders is selling 3.38 million shares, or about $280 million apiece at $83, roughly $2 billion combined. Not bad for a company whose prospectus warns of "existential risks to humanity."

Six Times Covered (By Whom?)

The demand story is real, at least on paper. Bloomberg reported the book was "multiple times" oversubscribed within a day of launch, then about six times, with multiple orders of $10 billion or more. Up to 20% of the deal is going to retail, and Vanda Research expects about $250 million of net retail buying on day one, twice what it saw for SpaceX. According to the WSJ, venture backers including Bessemer, Menlo and Accel planned to add to their stakes in the offering rather than sell.

But as we cautioned last Wednesday, oversubscription is a marketing number and guarantees nothing about performance: Klarna and StubHub were both heavily oversubscribed and both broke issue, and Cerebras was about 20x covered. It is now trading at a fraction of its IPO price. 

Then there's the $26 billion of Class N stock going to seven companies at the IPO price: Google and Nvidia ($10 billion each), AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC. Of course, since each one of them also sells Anthropic its chips or cloud, expect that $26 billion to be promptly "circularly refinanced" right back to the companies who "invested it.". At $83 that's about 313 million shares, and since Google's $10 billion funds a commitment it had already made, the "new" money is probably closer to $16 billion (or $0 after payment for chips). Nothing says arm's-length price discovery like your vendors setting the floor.

And the vendor relationship doesn't stop at the cap table. Nearly half of Anthropic's revenue is sold through the hyperscalers' own cloud marketplaces, which also account for the majority of its receivables:

What $83 Buys You

The bull case boils down to one number: an $81 billion revenue run rate as of Oct. 31, up $10 billion in a single month (it is unclear if Dario is annualizing days now, or has moved on to hours or maybe even minutes for the biggest pig-lipstick boost possible). At $83, buyers are paying 18.4x that run rate fully diluted (13.4x on shares outstanding). At $2 trillion it would have been 25x, which is about the only sense in which this is a bargain.

The rest of the amended S-1 is less flattering, as we detailed when the prospectus dropped and again at launch:

  • Q3 revenue rose 47% sequentially to $16.96 billion, down from 144% growth in Q2;
  • a $567 million operating loss, one quarter after the first-ever $974 million operating profit, blamed on $5 billion of pricier short-term compute;
  • price cuts and discounts shaved about $600 million off Q3 revenue;
  • and nearly $901 billion of commitments, mostly compute.

The operating leverage story reversed in a single quarter: total operating expenses climbed back to 103% of revenue, as compute and infrastructure jumped to 58% of sales from 48%...

...which means each dollar of compute bought less revenue for the first time in the series: $1.72 in Q3, down from $2.08.

So much for the first-ever operating profit. One and done, at least for now:

And then there's the bill. Add up the contractual obligations table, signed leases that haven't started, post-Sept 30 deals and short-term commitments and you get $895.4 billion of committed spend in the S-1/A, plus an estimated $150-175 billion under deals with no fixed dollar amount. That's a trillion-dollar tab.

Of that, $69.8 billion is due in the next 12 months, more than Q3's annualized revenue and roughly 11x nine-month operating cash flow:

Put differently, the roughly $92.5 billion Anthropic will pocket from the IPO and the placement (before the upsize and the greenshoe) covers about 16 months of bills already signed, and about one-tenth of the total. And, as noted above, a good chunk of it goes right back to the same seven companies that just bought the biggest chunk of stock. Even the lead-left bank's own model (per the FT) sees free cash outflows of $65.7 billion in 2027 and operating losses peaking around $40 billion before turning positive in 2029, on the way to $600 billion of revenue by 2030. Which, well, is a lot of things that have to go right.

Votes Here, Money There

Public buyers at $83 are also buying into the structure we drew up last month: a single Class F share gives the seven founders a fixed 50.1% of the vote, the Long-Term Benefit Trust's single Class T share picks four of the seven directors, and Class A holders are capped at 49.9% with no practical say over a single board seat. Amazon and Google own up to 12% and 14.99% with zero votes, and every Class N stake converts to Class A the moment it's sold, with registration rights to match.

Translation: the overhang is built in. On top of the usual lock-up expiries, the Public Benefit Fund gets up to another 2% of the company every time the stock rises 50% from the IPO price, so the first trigger sits at $124.50. In other words, the dilution kicks in precisely when the stock is working.

Making Room For ANT

The deal has already moved markets. As we noted in today's wrap, desk chatter suggested much of the recent price action was about making room for Anthropic, with gold, crypto, copper and Nvidia all puked to fund allocations. That came on top of Nomura's Charlie McElligott flagging dealers at their most short gamma since 2019 heading into his NVDA-Anthropic-OpEx "risk quad-fecta."

As for Thursday's open, the crypto crowd has already placed its bets: Hyperliquid's pre-IPO perp traded near $99 on Tuesday, about 19% above tonight's offer price. Given the book, the retail allocation and the race to launch leveraged ANT ETFs, a first-day pop looks about as close to a sure thing as these things get. What happens after is a different question.

Enter Warren

Washington also weighed in, just in time for pricing. Minutes after the $85 headline, Sen. Elizabeth Warren took aim at the deal, seizing on the same "existential risks to humanity" language from the prospectus that we flagged at launch, and warning about "potential threats to Americans' retirements and the entire financial system if this IPO goes awry":

The timing is a little late: the S-1 has been public since Oct. 26 and the books closed Tuesday at 4pm. Funny how the existential risk only became a regulatory emergency a few hours before pricing. Still, the "retirements" angle isn't entirely wrong: with up to 20% of the deal earmarked for retail and leveraged single-stock ETFs lining up, Main Street will own a lot of this stock very quickly, probably at well above $83.

The Benchmark Nobody Can Ignore

H.C. Wainwright's Mike Colonnese called a successful Anthropic IPO "an important valuation benchmark for the AI sector," and he's right. Peter Thiel's Jack Selby put the other side bluntly:

"An underperforming Anthropic IPO has to be a very prominent player in what will be a pretty massive correction in the market with respect to AI... just imagine where it's going to go after the lockups expire."

Here's our take. The pop is the easy part: a six-times-covered book, a fifth of the deal in retail hands and a market that sold everything else to make room all but guarantee a strong open. The hard part starts afterwards, when the vendor stakes, the Public Benefit Fund and the lock-up expiries begin feeding supply into a float that just absorbed a record $94 billion, at 18x a run rate whose growth halved last quarter and against a compute bill that runs to the better part of a trillion dollars. Bankers priced this for a pop; the risk is everything after it. We know which way we lean.

Or, as we put it when the $85 whisper hit this afternoon:

We'll find out at Thursday's open.

items.title: AI Is Outrunning America's Cyber Defenses, And Washington Has No Plan To Catch Up
items.content_text:
AI Is Outrunning America's Cyber Defenses, And Washington Has No Plan To Catch Up

Two senators, one Democrat and one Republican, warned the Trump administration on Wednesday that AI-enabled cyber threats are "rapidly escalating" and outpacing America's defenses.

Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-WA) and Mike Rounds (R-SD) sent the warning in a letter to Jay Clayton, chair of the White House Super Intelligence Task Force. They urged immediate action to protect critical infrastructure, financial institutions and widely used software.

The letter follows a week of technology failures that reached airports, tech companies, media, and even banks. A Microsoft outage took down email and other services. U.S. air travel came to a halt. A software problem at JPMorgan Chase hit banking services.

The administration has rejected the idea that foreign hackers caused the disruptions. Instead, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has pointed to artificial intelligence as a possible cause, including the problem that grounded every U.S. flight for hours last week.

Mullin told Fox News he had spoken with someone in the tech industry whom he declined to name. He confirmed the person was not Tesla CEO Elon Musk. According to Mullin, his source said brand-new AI running on outdated systems could be driving the outages.

"He said, 'I believe it's SI, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is,'" Mullin said.

He then described how his source thinks the failures spread. "So when they put in a program that's able to write code, it goes in and self-fixes itself, as it starts to self-fix itself, like a change order on a house," Mullin said. "When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing as a ripple effect."

"It causes the systems to be overrun that weren't designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today," he said. "That was the conversation I had today. That kind of makes sense to me."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Nov. 15, a day before Mullin's remarks, that there was "no possible way" the FAA's AI planning platform played a role in the ground stop, which was traced to a router upgrade at a remote radio site in Arkansas. Microsoft said its outage was not caused by AI or a cyberattack but by "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade," and JPMorgan said there was no evidence its outage was cyber-related.

Cantwell and Rounds say the danger extends beyond any single outage. In their letter, they described an attacker's advantage that grows by the month.

"AI is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software and our defenses are not keeping pace," the senators wrote.

They called for faster deployment of defensive AI tools and strong security standards for autonomous AI agents, software that can act on its own across networks and systems.

The letter cited several recent incidents. AI found flaws in PHP, one of the internet's most widely used programming languages. After the flaws became public last month, government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline. The senators also pointed to rogue AI disrupting banking services and to data breaches at Japanese companies.

One case involved China. Toronto-based AI firm Cohere reported that a Chinese-developed Qwen model tried to make an unauthorized connection to a server in China during testing, according to the letter. The senators noted the episode does not establish deliberate malicious behavior, and Cohere said the attempt was blocked because its test environment had no internet connection.

Wednesday's letter marks the second time the pair has pressed Clayton in recent weeks. Last month, Cantwell and Rounds sent him a separate letter asking for a comprehensive national AI safety and cyber defense strategy.

The industry's own leaders have raised alarms. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Musk have called for a coordinated slowdown in AI development. Their calls followed incidents such as the OpenAI-Hugging Face episode, in which an AI swarm carried out cyberattacks.

The senators argued that private companies cannot handle the threat on their own and that the federal government must take the lead.

"We cannot meet these threats with yesterday's cyber security infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy," Cantwell and Rounds wrote.

Industry experts told the New York Post that the simultaneous outages are no coincidence. Companies that run the backbone of the digital economy are racing to bolt new AI tools onto complex and often outdated computer systems before the holidays, when spending climbs and more employees take time off. The experts warned the failures could get worse before they get better.

items.title: Trump Admin To Permanently Cut Off Los Angeles Homelessness Agency
items.content_text:
Trump Admin To Permanently Cut Off Los Angeles Homelessness Agency

Authored by Naveen Athrappully via The Epoch Times,

The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) is permanently ending funding for a major Los Angeles agency tackling homelessness as part of a settlement agreement over fraud allegations.

The Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) is the lead agency for homelessness response in Los Angeles. The department suspended payments to LAHSA in June after the HUD Office of Inspector General uncovered "overwhelming evidence of LAHSA's record of fraud, failure and flagrant mismanagement" at the organization.

LAHSA filed a lawsuit, and has now reached a settlement that "requires LAHSA to hand over about $150 million in federal funding and permanently be severed from HUD's homelessness funding by the end of 2027," HUD said in a Nov. 17 statement.

🚨 It's official: LAHSA is cut off.

In a landmark settlement, they agreed to never take another tax dollar from HUD.

Under @POTUS and @WHFraudTF, we promised to root out fraud from the homeless industrial complex, and we are delivering. pic.twitter.com/nCA1i0PrwX

— Scott Turner (@SecretaryTurner) November 17, 2026

The Los Angeles Continuum of Care, a body of stakeholders that coordinates homelessness response in the region, had received almost $1 billion in government funding over the last five years, HUD said in a June 11 statement. The Continuum of Care is led by LAHSA.

"Despite receiving more federal homelessness funding than any other jurisdiction in the nation, Los Angeles remains the epicenter of the nation's drug-fueled homelessness crisis," the department said.

Homelessness in Los Angeles has doubled while the region's funding nearly tripled since 2013, according to HUD.

HUD said it uncovered a "clear pattern of fraud" at LAHSA. In one instance, it said, the organization failed to provide documentation to verify the existence of almost 2,300 housing sites. In another instance, LAHSA was allegedly unable to determine whether it had used taxpayer funds to pay for empty hotel rooms as the organization failed to record whether beneficiaries had left, the department said.

With funding for LAHSA permanently terminated by the end of next year, Los Angeles County will take over LAHSA's projects in the region, which will be overseen by HUD, the department said in the latest statement.

"Under President [Donald] Trump's leadership, HUD will fund results, not corruption and gross incompetence," HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in the statement.

"Year after year, LAHSA funneled billions of dollars in federal funding to organizations with no oversight, which resulted in nothing but skyrocketing homelessness, failing at their most basic responsibility," Turner said. "Taxpayers will no longer bankroll an organization that fails to deliver for the Americans it was created to serve."

During litigation, LAHSA maintained that HUD's funding suspension in June was "unlawful and represented federal overreach," the organization said in a Nov. 17 statement.

Gita O'Neill, interim chief executive officer of LAHSA, said the settlement "closes a difficult chapter" for the organization.

"From the outset, we have maintained that LAHSA did not engage in wrongdoing and that HUD's suspension lacked a legal foundation," O'Neill said. "We stood firm in defending LAHSA, the Los Angeles Continuum of Care, and the importance of local decision-making in our region's homelessness response."

"Our focus now is on working closely with our local partners to ensure continuity of services, support an orderly transition, and remain true to our mission of connecting our unhoused neighbors with the services, resources, and pathways to housing they need," O'Neill said.

There were an estimated 73,040 homeless people in Los Angeles County this year, according to a July report from LAHSA. This is up by 1.2 percent from the previous year, with the uptick breaking two consecutive years of decline. Los Angeles City alone is home to 45,194 homeless people.

Meanwhile, HUD announced a 6.3 percent annual nationwide decrease in homelessness in a Nov. 6 statement.

On a single night in January this year, 698,425 individuals were homeless, which was 6.3 percent fewer than in January last year when President Donald Trump took over White House, HUD said, adding that this was the largest annual decline on record.

"President Trump's actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Turner said in the statement.

"Any Pretty Woman That Comes From China, They Consider Her To Be A Spy": Trump Waves Off Jensen Scandal

President Trump brushed off the scandal that ended Jensen Huang's run at Nvidia, telling Fox News in Shenzhen that the woman at the center of it was a businesswoman, not a spy.

"It was a pretty woman. And any pretty woman that comes from China, they consider her to be a spy," Trump told Fox's Jacqui Heinrich in an interview that aired Wednesday night on The Ingraham Angle.

"I haven't heard that she was a spy," he said of Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman whose affair with the former CEO set off an internal probe at Nvidia. "She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong."

Asked whether he raised Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping over dinner, Trump said: "We did not discuss it. I might have referred to it just briefly because it's such a tragedy." The two leaders talked about artificial intelligence the whole evening, he said.

TRUMP on Jensen Huang's ousting: "Such a tragedy."

President Trump reacts to the former NVIDIA CEO's departure during an interview with @JacquiHeinrich, calling him "a brilliant man."

"Some people can't be replaced. He was ten years ahead," Trump says, adding that he briefly... pic.twitter.com/S62N44GWVv

— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 19, 2026

Trump called Huang "such a brilliant man" and, pointing to Elon Musk, argued the country owes its rare talents protection: "We have to take care of our geniuses. By the way, we don't have that many of them." He added: "I helped Elon a lot in my first term. A lot of people don't know that you wouldn't probably have Elon today."

"We have to take care of our geniuses."

President Trump points to Elon Musk as a prime example of why America needs to back its brightest innovators, emphasizing the support he says he gave the billionaire during his first administration.

Speaking with @JacquiHeinrich ahead of... pic.twitter.com/9kad5YI0IB

Nvidia said with its third-quarter results that it won't reinstate Huang, after Huang said he owns his mistakes and would return if asked, while the SEC opened another probe of the company.

House committees plan to question Huang behind closed doors on Dec. 1 about his ties to the suspected spy and Nvidia's chip sales, Fox News reported, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Wednesday he was never briefed on the relationship, which he said was handled outside his department.

Police 'Examining' Claims Epstein Trafficked Women On The King's Balmoral Estate

Scotland's top police officer has confirmed that her force is examining claims that women were trafficked by Jeffrey Epstein on Balmoral, the King's private estate in Aberdeenshire, in a probe that also covers the time Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor spent there with Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.

Asked by Sky News Scotland correspondent Connor Gillies whether the inquiry concerns "trafficking, or not, of women on the Balmoral estate involving Jeffrey Epstein and the former Prince Andrew," Police Scotland Chief Constable Jo Farrell said: "So, that's information that we've received from parties and we're examining it."

"We will progress that and determine what action needs to be... taken," Farrell said in her first public comments since the allegations emerged. "When I can share more information, we will."

According to Sky, it is the first time police have publicly confirmed that the Balmoral probe is examining an allegation of trafficking involving the King's brother and Epstein.

Until now, Police Scotland had only confirmed, on Oct. 30, that it had received "information" and had "active enquiries ongoing" into the time spent at Balmoral, at what it called "a very early stage." The force has not said what the information was or what offense, if any, it suspects, and it has named no suspect.

The Scottish Daily Express first reported that the inquiry related to claims women were "trafficked" to Balmoral. Andrew reportedly invited Epstein to the estate in 1999, and photos released by the US Justice Department appear to show Epstein and Maxwell there. Flight logs show Andrew and Maxwell flying from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's jet on Sept. 1, 2006, according to UPI. The Scottish inquiry followed a public appeal by Police Scotland in February for information about Epstein's use of Edinburgh Airport.

Maxwell is serving a 20-year US prison sentence for sex trafficking. Epstein died in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

Balmoral is one of several fronts in the UK: Thames Valley Police arrested Andrew on suspicion of misconduct in public office on Feb. 19, his 66th birthday, over allegations he shared sensitive information with Epstein while serving as the UK's trade envoy.

The same force said in May it had "engaged with" the legal representative of a woman who says she was trafficked to Andrew's former home, Royal Lodge, in 2010, when she was 20, according to the Irish Times.

The Metropolitan Police and Surrey Police also have live investigations linked to the release of the Epstein files, the National Police Chiefs' Council has said. King Charles stripped his brother of his prince title and his dukedom last year over his association with Epstein.

Andrew, who was interviewed under caution and released under investigation after his arrest, has always denied any wrongdoing.

items.title: APEC-ing Order
items.content_text:
APEC-ing Order

By Michael Every of Rabobank

Today is all about APEC-ing order.

Starting with markets, Anthropic raised $81bn in a record IPO, showing AI is still the apex trade even when the firm involved may present a potential risk to the existence of humanity. Either “because markets” or national security, or both, it seems.

Next to monetary policy, where the October FOMC minutes backed further rate hikes and Waller called for the apex central bank to make a 50bps hike in December, boosting the US dollar. Further down the chain, the Bank of Canada said scenarios help make monetary policy more effective: but what if the scenarios are wildly variant depending on geopolitical outcomes that central banks have no influence over? The RBA now faces an Aussie economy where unemployment is spiking (from 4.7% to 4.9%) and jobs growth was -43.5K vs. an expected +25K, making further rate hikes less likely even as the October CPI print next week could still show a sharp headline lift. But what if geopolitics goes south regardless of the labor market?

APEC saw Trump greeted by Xi Jinping with a hug and pom-poms while Putin was met by a lower level, taller Chinese official, which looked a deliberate diplomatic snub. Today, the three men meet in a ‘smoke-filled room.’ The EU isn’t in Asia, so can’t attend, but probably wouldn’t have been able to send one person into that room based on the seven-strong team it offered when the US asked for a negotiator (singular) for Russia. The global pecking order is clear. 

The Financial Times thinks this meeting is irrelevant. Politico calls it ‘An absolute nightmare.’ The Telegraph proclaims, ‘The meeting that could mark the end of the world as we know it.’ Even a partial ‘Yalta’ could have huge consequences for geopolitics, geoeconomics, and markets – and for central banks. 

So could any failure to agree on anything. Some say Trump’s push for a tripartite denuclearisation deal --he just said the US doesn’t need 4,000 nukes, just 10(!)-- likely won’t be agreed to by Russia or China. More importantly, can the three find a way to de-escalate the rising, conflating geopolitical and geoeconomic tensions on multiple fronts?

That’s hard given the US is torn over its approach to China, clear not just in the Nvidia affair, still rumbling on, but in a new report handed to Congress arguing Beijing is using Trump-Xi “stability” to build a strategic edge. Calls are growing for even tighter controls on the sale of AI chips to China and third parties; Congress is asking Microsoft to explain its new $500m Open AI deal talks with China’s ByteDance; the White House is reportedly weighing an executive order forcing US firms to disclose their level of Chinese AI use; and the Dutch government has objected to an “unacceptable” bipartisan US Congressional MATCH Act that would limit ASML’s semiconductor sales to China. (In which case, what might the Dutch or EU response be, and with what consequences?)

The US-China trade truce where rare earths flow to the US, in constrained volumes, expires 10 January. While the US is seen as highly unlikely to catch China up on rare earths in 10 months, as Trump just claimed, its recent statecraft efforts are seen as starting to slowly pay off both at home and via new non-China deals abroad. So, what happens next?

The US also warned the window to push for a Ukraine ceasefire is closing, likely with the new Congress. After that, war may escalate and the US may deescalate its support - via a Trump veto if needed. Indeed, following Ukraine hitting the Kerch bridge with new tech avoiding US systems, the Pentagon chief walked out of NATO talks after admonishing Kyiv.

The New York Times reports Trump is weighing new strikes on Iran, which may take down civilian infrastructure like electricity. That could unleash matching destruction in the GCC. The Times also says Trump is frustrated with VP Vance’s public critique of the Iran War; Trump just publicly stated it was the right thing to do, regardless of elections, and he would do the same again. Congress was just told that the cost of insuring a ship through Hormuz has risen from around $54,000 to $64m, which a maritime expert says translates into expectations of one ship in 20 being sunk; that’s as the Saudis made clear they expect their war with the Houthis to last at least six more months, and as Ethiopia and Eritrea have amassed forces along their border, heightening war fears there.

Would a new US attack have a sign-off from Putin and Xi – if so, for what quid pro quo on other fronts? If not, would it point to no ‘Yalta’ and so to even broader escalation? 

Showing how pieces on the board in this Great Game can move, US Secretary of War Hegseth cemented a US-Venezuela military deal to establish a US base and train troops. He’s in Colombia today as troops from Trump ally El Salvador continue to take out the gangs of Haiti, potentially bringing that country into the Donroe Doctrine. 

Who else, where else could be next, in either direction?

In more gentlemanly economic statecraft, ahead of tomorrow’s EU-UK summit, the EU is reported to have told PM Burnham there will be no more deals without rejoining the single market. That at least brings matters to a head for the UK. But which direction will it then head in?

France blocked an EU law that could see the EU sovereign spectrum opened up to SpaceX and Amazon; EU governments approved a trade deal with Indonesia; Trump announced $17bn in US FDI into the Philippines; a Korea-China FTA deal on services and investment advanced as groundwork for deeper economic ties; and Canadian PM Carney contrasted “very professional” Chinese trade talks with a still-elusive US deal, also pitching his proposed Pacific Link crude pipeline to Asian leaders – as a Canadian paper bewailed ‘An exodus of innovators’ to the US. 

The South China Morning Post asks, ‘Sign of the times? How China is quietly shifting global trade onto yuan payments’, though the fact that Russia has given up on that CNY-as-a-dollar-alternative approach speaks volumes about the practical limits of such a policy… at least for now.

Where does what you cover or care about stand in APEC-ing order?

items.title: Short Seller Comes For AMD's "China Problem" - But Read The Fine Print
items.content_text:
Short Seller Comes For AMD's "China Problem" - But Read The Fine Print

AMD responded to the report just a few minutes ago, saying in a statement that they comply with US export control laws, and that Hunterbrook's claims "misrepresent AMD's practices." More to come...

***

A week after Wall Street crowned AMD the big winner of Nvidia's China crisis, a short seller is out with quite the bear case. Hunterbrook Media, whose affiliated fund is short AMD, published an investigation Thursday arguing that AMD has "a China problem of its own," built on AMD firmware turning up at a blacklisted Chinese server maker and three companies tied to it.

Investors treated $AMD as the winner of Nvidia's China crisis.

The problem: AMD has a China problem of its own.

Our investigation: pic.twitter.com/9AR6HGgEhx

— Hunterbrook (@hntrbrkmedia) November 19, 2026

Except further down, Hunterbrook says the records it found "don't establish on their own a violation of export laws," that it doesn't know how the blacklisted company got AMD's code, and that AMD's other ties to blacklisted firms are "relatively small given the size and scope of AMD's business."

AMD rose 4% the morning Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Nov. 12, capping a week in which the stock gained almost 50%, before it dropped 10.8% early the next day. Hunterbrook's pitch is that investors who rotated from Nvidia into AMD bought a pricier stock with the same China risk. 

The blacklisted company is IEIT Systems, an arm of Inspur Group, which is controlled by Shandong province's state-assets regulator. The Commerce Department put IEIT on its Entity List in March 2025, two years after blacklisting Inspur Group itself, so shipping IEIT anything covered by US export rules takes a license that Commerce's stated policy is to deny.

Hunterbrook downloaded IEIT's server software and found AMD's startup code inside. Since the blacklisting, IEIT has built at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its own updates, most recently in one it posted Oct. 19, about one to two months after AMD's releases. One October 2025 update carried a fix for a flaw AMD didn't disclose publicly until Feb. 24, 2026.

How IEIT got the code isn't exactly clear. Hunterbrook found the same code on the public download pages of three server sellers that aren't blacklisted, which is where it got those files itself, and says it doesn't know whether AMD or anyone else held a license to supply IEIT. William Reinsch, a former Commerce undersecretary for export administration, told Hunterbrook that "the fact that you have to get a license does not mean automatically that the license will be denied." Commerce doesn't make those licenses public.

The precedent Hunterbrook cites is Lambda Research, a Massachusetts software maker that Commerce settled with in October for sending its own automatic updates to China's SiCarrier after it was blacklisted, seven violations in all. The fine, Hunterbrook notes, was small, and Lambda sent the updates itself, while Hunterbrook doesn't say who passed AMD's code to IEIT.

The three sellers are Maginfra in China, Kaytus in Singapore and Aivres in Fremont, California. Hunterbrook found their firmware files 99.94% identical to IEIT's, all seemingly for one AMD server design that Aivres and Kaytus both sell as the KR2280-E3, and corporate filings tie them to IEIT: Kaytus's audited 2025 accounts name IEIT as its ultimate holding company, Aivres was called Inspur Systems until May 2023, and IEIT's 2022 annual report lists it as a subsidiary.

None of the three is on the Entity List, so selling them AMD gear takes no blacklist license today. AMD's website lists Aivres among the makers of servers built on its Instinct AI accelerators, and Aivres is a sponsor of AMD's Advancing AI 2026 conference. Aivres has also surfaced in the Nvidia saga: the New York Times reported in September that it exported at least $5.6 billion of advanced technology to Southeast Asia between April 2024 and February, more than $3 billion of it computers built with Nvidia chips.

US customs records show 209 ocean shipments of server parts reaching Aivres from China since IEIT's blacklisting, mostly boards, cases and power supplies without chips. Hunterbrook says the records don't show whose chips went into the finished machines or where they were shipped. An Aivres operations manager who gave his name as John told a Hunterbrook reporter in Fremont on Nov. 17, "I can say we ship a lot to China and neighboring countries."

The bear case leans on rules that haven't bitten yet (like that?). A Commerce rule extending blacklist restrictions to any foreign company at least 50% owned by a listed entity could catch Kaytus, but it's on hold: Commerce issued it in September 2025, suspended it last November, and on Nov. 9 extended the suspension through Jan. 10, 2027.

The other rule, the one Commerce released Monday, takes effect today and requires licenses for advanced AI chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, except to US-headquartered buyers. AMD billed $4.28 billion to customers in Singapore in fiscal 2025, or 12.4% of revenue, and $7.75 billion, or 22.4%, to China and Hong Kong, according to its annual report. Hunterbrook sets that against Nvidia's 9.1%, though Nvidia's figure counts customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong, while AMD's counts where customers are billed.

AMD also reported $67 million of "licensing gain" in 2025, which Hunterbrook traces to two Chengdu chip ventures with Hygon that Commerce blacklisted in 2019; Hygon's filings imply about $270 million paid over 2021-2025, close to the $263 million AMD reported. That $67 million is about 0.2% of AMD's $34.6 billion in 2025 revenue, and the Entity List restricts exports to listed companies, not payments from them.

Meanwhile, two ventures 85% owned by China's Tongfu Microelectronics do most of AMD's chip assembly, testing and packaging, and AMD bought $2 billion of services from them in 2025. That arrangement is a decade old: AMD sold 85% of its Suzhou and Penang plants to Nantong Fujitsu Microelectronics, now Tongfu, in 2016 and kept 15%. AMD also lent one venture $100 million in October 2024, a loan still outstanding at the end of September.

Where AMD is exposed is the growth story: its Instinct AI accelerators already need a license to ship to China, and when Washington put that requirement on AMD's China-specific MI308 in April 2025, AMD warned of up to about $800 million in charges. Congress, meanwhile, has opened probes into how Nvidia's exports to Chinese companies were approved, not AMD's.

Shares were down sharply Thursday morning amid this, and a general Anthropic IPO day barf-fest - with a bounce in the works as of this writing.

items.title: Google Signs Landmark Superhot Geothermal Deal
items.content_text:
Google Signs Landmark Superhot Geothermal Deal

Authored by Tsvetana Paraskova via OilPrice.com,

  • Google has signed a landmark 50-MW geothermal power deal with Quaise Energy, targeting electricity from superhot rocks in Oregon for its data centers starting in the early 2030s. 
  • Breakthrough drilling technologies could transform geothermal economics, with superhot rock potentially delivering 10 times more power per well than conventional geothermal systems. 
  • AI's soaring electricity demand is accelerating geothermal investment, as global data center power consumption is projected to surge 170% between 2025 and 2030.

The AI boom and the hyperscalers' need for round-the-clock clean energy for their data centers meet the next-generation geothermal energy technologies developed by a number of start-ups.

In a world first, Google this week signed an agreement with Quaise Energy to use power from the superhot rocks in the Newberry Volcano in Oregon for its existing data center operations in The Dalles.

Quaise Energy, which develops utility-scale superhot geothermal energy, has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) under which Google will buy 50 megawatts (MW) of superhot geothermal power from Project Obsidian, Quaise's flagship project in Central Oregon, beginning in the early 2030s.

Quaise Energy says this first-of-its-kind deal will help catalyze the commercial development of superhot geothermal energy.

Traditional geothermal energy is limited to regions with naturally occurring hot-water reservoirs that rarely exceed 600 degrees F. But superhot rock is a kind of enhanced geothermal that digs miles into the Earth to reach temperatures of nearly 800 F. Once superhot temperatures are reached, cold water is injected to create steam, which powers turbines.

Quaise Energy says superhot geothermal is a virtually limitless energy source that uses the Earth's natural heat to generate up to 10 times more clean power per well than traditional geothermal systems.

At Project Obsidian, the company expects to be the first in the world to use millimeter wave drilling, a technology that can plug into existing drilling rigs to economically reach superhot geothermal conditions.

Millimeter wave drilling is the keystone of superhot geothermal, Quaise Energy says, noting it is the only way to access the resource at scale while reaching economic and power parity with fossil fuels.

"Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power," Quaise Energy's CEO and president Carlos Araque said in a statement.

For Google, the agreement is more than just another PPA for clean energy as the tech giant built its first owned-and-operated data center in The Dalles, Oregon, in 2006.

Oregon's Newberry is also the site of a superhot geothermal project under development by another start-up, Mazama Energy, which just this week announced a first-of-its-kind chilling technology to protect critical equipment in 645°F superhot rock while increasing drilling speed by 20%. These breakthroughs address key barriers to competitive geothermal power, Mazama Energy says.

"We can now address geothermal economics from both directions: lowering the cost of drilling each well and accessing hotter rock that can deliver far more energy," Mazama Energy's chief executive officer Sriram Vasantharajan said.

"That is how utility-scale geothermal can become a truly competitive source of firm power."

Mazama in September raised $135 million in new capital to accelerate superhot rock geothermal commercial development, with strategic investors Shell Ventures and ConocoPhillips alongside John Arnold's Centaurus Capital, Doerr Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Gates Frontier.

Recent breakthroughs and growing interest from AI hyperscalers could supercharge superhot rock geothermal development.

The Clean Air Task Force estimates that just 1% of the superhot rock (SHR) geothermal potential in the United States could produce 4.3 terawatts (TW) of firm, flexible power. That's nearly four times the current total installed electricity-generating capacity in the United States.

Superhot rock geothermal energy could help meet part of the soaring power demand from data centers while providing 24/7 clean energy to the hyperscalers' facilities.

Goldman Sachs Research last month said that it now expects global data center power demand to soar by 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of that growth coming from within the United States.

"Power is probably the forever bottleneck," said Jason Tofsky, global head of Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking at Goldman Sachs.

items.title: "Today Feels Important...": US Equity Indices Plunge As Anthropic Open Looms
items.content_text:
"Today Feels Important...": US Equity Indices Plunge As Anthropic Open Looms

Update (1045ET): Unfortunately for Goldman's Rich Privorotsky, the early squeeze in stocks has faded very rapidly. As the indicative price for Anthropic's IPO open increases (latest around $105 from $83 IPO), so the US Majors have tumbled since the US cash market opened...

...and SPX has broken back below its 200DMA...

~~~~~

The biggest IPO in history opens on the Nasdaq this morning, and hedge funds have rarely owned less of the sector it belongs to.

Per Goldman Prime, the hedge fund book's net weight in tech has slumped to roughly 18%, against a 29% weight in the index: an 11-point underweight, roughly matching the deepest levels in five years and a stunning reversal from mid-2026, when the pros were briefly overweight the sector. Which is why Goldman's head of EMEA Delta One trading Rich Privorotsky titled his Thursday morning note "Pivotal. Rates Resilient. Heavy Tech Selling." (available to pro subs), and opened his risk section with three words:

"Today feels important. SPX precariously holding its 200d, street gamma positioning is meant to be very short but vol was soggy yesterday for the first time in a while (particularly post VIX expiry). With VIX in the mid 20s and Thanksgiving next week, there is a meaningful potential tailwind if the market can simply stabilize. Stability can beget stability."

In other words, the selling has gone so far that merely not falling could be enough to spark a squeeze. And with Nasdaq futures up nearly 2% this morning on the back of Anthropic's above-range pricing, today is the test.

"Doesn't Take Much Good News To Squeeze"

The overnight picture was less festive outside the US. Privorotsky notes America "absorbed plenty of bad news yesterday, but Asia struggling": Goldman's TSMC-exposed basket is down 8%, and Asian data center names are under pressure. The culprit is the Commerce Department's new BIS rule, which we covered earlier this week: it requires licenses for advanced chip shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and for any data center anywhere selling more than 12 million TPP of compute to China-parented customers (offshore operators already doing so get 90 days to get a license or wind it down). Per Privorotsky, the BIS rules mean "delayed projects, displaced demand and excess infrastructure capacity. Hard to quantify, but clearly was not fully priced in Asia."

Translation: the Johor and Singapore data center boom, built in no small part to rent GPUs to Chinese customers who couldn't buy them, just lost its best customer. (The first domino, a frozen $480 million loan linked to ByteDance, has already fallen.)

And yet, Privorotsky points out, the offset is positioning:

"The offset is positioning… two months of aggressive selling have left valuations depressed across global semis. Doesn't take much good news to squeeze, and although the BIS implications may not be fully digested in parts of Asia supply chain, if they can be compartmentalized that's encouraging."

Here is how depressed: the chart below, from Goldman's prime brokerage analytics team, tracks the PB book's net weight in tech (blue) against the sector's index weight (orange). The teal line, the over/underweight, has swung from roughly +2% at the June peak to -11% as of Monday (all levels read off the chart, so approximate):

Goldman's PB team made the same point in its latest chart pack, titled "Fundamental L/S Net Exposure Below Liberation Day Lows. Value Rotation." Put differently, funds have spent two months selling the AI trade and buying everything else, and when you are that short relative to the benchmark, a single good day for tech forces a lot of people to chase. Diversification at its finest.

Hawkish Waller, Hawkish Minutes... And Bonds Rallied Anyway

The other thing that caught Privorotsky's eye was the bond market's refusal to panic. Wednesday served up Waller reprising his 50bps hike call, minutes showing "almost all" FOMC members see more hikes, plus some ECB regulatory noise. The response:

"Hawkish Waller, Fed minutes and ECB regulatory noise, yet bonds rallied. Back end well bid, curve bull flattening, front end broadly unchanged. Australia particularly interesting… big jobs miss, 2yr rallying hard and cuts starting to price... now potentially signaling the end of hiking cycle."

"Big jobs miss" is putting it politely. Australia lost 43,500 jobs in October, against expectations for a 25,000 gain, after losing 39,300 in September, and unemployment jumped to 4.9%, the highest since 2021. Two straight months of job losses after a string of RBA hikes: so much for the soft landing Down Under.

Privorotsky sees the global bond market doing the Fed's thinking for it:

"Market is increasingly pricing weaker growth as capex expectations come down, commodities roll over and inflationary pressures appear to be fading. Feels like a lot of parallels to end of 2018. Same late cycle slowdown, very different policy implications. Rate price action was encouraging and suggests a lot of policy is already in the price. Internals of equity market very defensive and now commds pointing same direction."

Regular readers will recall that on Monday Privorotsky couldn't square equities pricing a slowdown while rates priced inflation, and by Wednesday he was buying front-end bonds alongside equities. A day later, the back end has joined the party, which means rates are finally pricing the same slowdown stocks have been pricing for weeks. One small detail: the 2018 parallel ended with a nearly 20% Christmas Eve crash before Powell blinked. Same late cycle, very different pain threshold, hopefully.

"Not A Savings Glut... It's A Spending Glut"

The commodity section of the note is the most interesting, mostly because it reads like an obituary for the reflation trade:

"Strong dollar, elevated real rates and attractive all in credit yields are providing competition for gold/precious. Not a savings glut...it's a spending glut, a less supportive backdrop for precious metals and multiples with the Fed tightening. China adds another headwind… weak growth, Shanghai equities near their lows and little sign of recovery. Potential restrictions on AI/data center investment compound the problem."

Then there's copper, which Privorotsky says "has become a proxy for that theme, making its resilience increasingly difficult to reconcile with collapsing AI infrastructure equities." Well, the reconciliation may have started: LME copper dropped 5% on Wednesday to its lowest since early April, with Druckenmiller short, CTAs dumping and only the actual copper users buying. Privorotsky acknowledges the "nuances around physical inventories, regional premiums and Chinese stockpiling," but his conclusion is blunt:

"Precious and industrial metals, grains, gasoline and diesel all under pressure. A broad disinflationary impulse that could materially change the rates narrative."

Gold, meanwhile, crashed below $3,800 on Wednesday, and was dumped alongside crypto as the dollar and bonds caught a bid. When the debasement trade, the AI trade and the China trade all unwind in the same week, the common denominator is probably liquidity. More on where that liquidity was going below.

Making Room For ANT

As we detailed last night, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, $5 above the top of the marketed $70-$78 range, and upsized the deal to 980 million shares from 825 million. That's $81.3 billion from the IPO, and $107.3 billion including the $26 billion vendor placement, 43% more than SpaceX's $75 billion in June and more than SK Hynix, Aramco, Alibaba and SoftBank combined:

Desk chatter all week suggested much of the gold, crypto, copper and Nvidia liquidation was about raising cash for exactly this allocation, which makes the "heavy tech selling" in Privorotsky's title and the record IPO two sides of the same trade. Back on Nov 12, we suspected as much:

marketwide gamma squeeze or the ANT IPO gets it.

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) November 12, 2026

Now that the money is spent, some of it may flow back. Futures are surging, chipmaker and Anthropic partner Broadcom (AVGO) was up 2.8% premarket, and Hyperliquid's pre-IPO perp traded near $99 on Tuesday, about 19% above the offer price. With a six-times-covered book, up to 20% of the deal in retail hands and Vanda expecting about $250 million of net retail buying on day one, a pop looks about as close to a sure thing as these things get.

What happens after is another matter. At $83 buyers are paying about 18x an $81 billion run rate fully diluted, for a company whose Q3 growth halved and which carries nearly $900 billion of committed spend, mostly compute, with $26 billion of its own stock sitting with the vendors who sell it that compute. Nothing says arm's-length price discovery like your chip suppliers setting the floor. Or, as we put it when the $85 whisper hit yesterday:

*ANTHROPIC IS SAID TO BE WEIGHING IPO PRICE UP TO $85 PER SHARE

so $70 on day two?

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) November 18, 2026

"An Awful Lot Is Now Reflected In Price"

Which brings us back to the 200-day. The S&P entered the week with dealers the most short gamma since 2019, and slipped under its long-term moving average on Tuesday:

S&P below the 200DMA for the first time since April

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) November 17, 2026

Privorotsky's closing argument is the most bullish thing he has written in weeks:

"I get the issues in AI… there are a myriad of them. But an awful lot is now reflected in price. If rates can play ball, there is a very real and legitimate bull case for equities. In hindsight the whole market changed when the Fed changed its posture… and it may well end the same way."

On today's docket, per Goldman:

  • Walmart (WMT) earnings, jobless claims and the Philly Fed;
  • a 10-year TIPS auction at 1pm ET;
  • the yen approaching 160 against the dollar ("watch," says Privorotsky);
  • "and obviously broader tech today," starting with ANT's first print.

Here's our take. The squeeze is the easy call: an 11-point tech underweight, short-gamma dealers, a record IPO pulling money back into AI and a holiday calendar that historically rewards anyone who can just sit tight. The harder part is the "if rates can play ball." The Fed's own minutes say almost everyone wants to hike more, and the disinflation Privorotsky is counting on is coming from collapsing commodities, Asian job losses and fading capex, which is usually what a slowdown looks like before it shows up in earnings. The 2018 analogy is apt; just remember that the market only got its Fed pivot after it forced one, and that the AI debt pile we have been warning about since last October was not around in 2018.

So yes, stability can beget stability. So can a pop, right up until the first lockup.

Much more in the full Goldman Delta One note, available to pro subs.

items.title: FAA Administrator Takes Blame For Nationwide Ground Stop
items.content_text:
FAA Administrator Takes Blame For Nationwide Ground Stop

Authored by Jacob Burg via The Epoch Times,

The chief of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) took the fall for last week's nationwide ground stop on Nov. 18, urging the public to blame him instead of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

"I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said regarding the ground stop. He spoke at an event on Nov. 18 hosted by The Hill and Airlines for America, an industry trade group.

"I wish people would lay off the secretary. He's got a lot of work to do, but I'm the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me if we need to blame somebody," Bedford said.

In multiple interviews and news conferences since Nov. 13, Duffy has reiterated that he would not apologize for instituting the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, which the FAA said was out of an abundance of caution. The more than four-hour halt to air traffic led to nearly 20,000 flight cancellations between the evening of Nov. 13 and the morning of Nov. 16.

Trump administration officials have said a network data overload precipitated the ground stop on a faulty router installed at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, as well as another installed weeks earlier at a Texas facility. The FAA announced on Nov. 17 that it would pause the installation of the new Juniper routers that the agency linked to the data overload when the device in Arkansas switched on during maintenance on Nov. 13.

Duffy has faced heat from lawmakers across the aisle, particularly after he asked Congress for a sizable sum - $50 billion - to overhaul the nation's aviation and air traffic control infrastructure.

Some have scrutinized the former congressman since last year's sweeping spending and tax-cut bill included $12.5 billion for aviation infrastructure, and much of it remains unspent.

The FAA also received an additional $1.9 billion from Congress early this year to modernize the agency's air traffic control system, which Democrats on the House Appropriations Committee highlighted in an X post on Nov. 15.

Of the full $14.4 billion that the FAA has received from Congress since July 2025, House Democrats say $9.1 billion remains unspent.

Thanking Duffy for meeting with Senate Republicans on Nov. 17, Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) said he agreed that the United States needs an updated air traffic control system, but that it "would cost about $10 billion."

"Congress has a role to play, but the airlines need to put up money and have skin in this game too. And yes, they can do it without raising ticket prices," Scott posted on X on Nov. 17.

Thank you, @SecDuffy, for coming to brief us today.

We absolutely need to update our air traffic control system, which would cost about $10 billion.

Congress has a role to play, but the airlines need to put up money and have skin in this game too. And yes, they can do it...

— Rick Scott (@SenRickScott) November 17, 2026

Bedford acknowledged the $50 billion funding request at the Nov. 18 trade group event.

"I think we're looking at this as a cost and it's [an] investment, and we need to rethink how this investment actually helps. And so the president and secretary said, 'Let's not do that,'" he said.

Bedford said President Donald Trump and Duffy said: "This is a call to action; we're going to fix the system, we're going to return to the gold standard. Let's do it right. Let's fix all of it."

items.title: Hackers Just Exposed Some Of JPMorgan's Richest Customers
items.content_text:
Hackers Just Exposed Some Of JPMorgan's Richest Customers

A ransomware gang calling itself n0n has published roughly 16,000 customer email addresses in a dataset apparently linked to JPMorgan Chase's invitation-only Reserve card program, according to Cybernews, whose researchers examined the release. Some records also contained phone numbers and account IDs.

The Reserve card is a Visa product for high-net-worth clients, typically associated with at least $10 million in assets managed by the bank, according to Cybernews. The outlet said the released dataset was only 502 KB, and it was unclear whether it represented a sample or everything the attackers had stolen.

JPMorgan separately confirmed a cyberattack on third-party service providers, saying in a statement posted to X that "third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack," and that "the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses." It has not named the vendors or confirmed n0n's responsibility, the 16,000 figure or the Reserve-program connection.

We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack. 

Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses....

— J.P. Morgan (@jpmorgan) November 19, 2026

"There is no disruption to our services," a JPMorgan spokesman said. "Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring." The bank said the breach was unrelated to the service disruption some customers experienced earlier in the week.

Then there's this: n0n added JPMorgan Chase to its leak site on Nov. 16, the same day Chase customers were hit by an outage, in a batch of 59 organizations across 11 countries that also named Visa and Mastercard, according to Breach News. The gang reportedly gave the named companies 48 hours to negotiate before it published.

At the time, JPMorgan pinned the outage on "a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" and said "there is no evidence it is cyber-related." The Treasury and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency called banks shortly after it was reported to confirm it was contained and not cyber-related, Reuters reported.

Visa has confirmed a cybersecurity incident at one of its own third-party providers, again unnamed, and said "Visa's systems were not involved and were not impacted" and that "there is no indication that payment data such as card numbers have been affected." Mastercard had made no public statement as of Breach News' report.

The reported connection to an elite card program could make the dataset especially useful to criminals seeking wealthy targets. Combined with other information, the exposed email addresses could help attackers identify individuals and craft more convincing phishing messages.

SOCRadar, which has tracked n0n since it surfaced in September, found an exposed staging server that month holding its attack scripts, its locker source code and an AI coding agent configured with 154 model entries across seven providers, including "uncensored" models and models with their safety training removed. The operators had spent more than $7,216 on AI services by Oct. 22.

As of Oct. 19, n0n listed 93 victims with ransom demands totaling $283.7 million. SOCRadar checked all 55 payment addresses it collected and found zero transactions as of Oct. 16.

JPMorgan is the latest big name in a bad week for corporate networks: a day earlier, the ransomware gang The Gentlemen claimed to have breached Nvidia. Nvidia said it was investigating a possible incident involving a third-party partner and had found no indication that its own systems or networks were affected, BleepingComputer reported. On Tuesday, the NSA, Apple and Equinor were all hit by disruptions as the FBI warned of state-aligned hackers.

None of n0n's earlier hits needed an exotic exploit: every compromise SOCRadar documented relied on weak or stolen credentials, including credential stuffing against 305 FortiGate VPN appliances.

Trump Warmly Greets 'My Friend' Putin, Who Says Ukraine Not Interested In Peace

President Vladimir Putin is in China meeting with Trump and Xi for their history-making trilateral summit, but while there was treated to reports of multiple Ukranainian strike waves on the strategic Crimean bridge this week. 

And so it is easy to see why Putin would conclude that Ukraine does not geniunely want to come to the peace table to make compromise. 

Speaking to reporters Thursday from Shenzhen, Putin reiterated that Moscow had agreed to compromises but that Zelensky is not a willing partner for peace. Crucially, this came after he was warmly greeted by President Trump in front of the cameras.

"We agreed to those compromise proposals as they were," Putin said, referencing conversations between he and Trump that go back to the Alaska summit. 

"The question is whether other parties to the conflict – in this case Ukraine and its European sponsors – want to agree to those proposals. Do they want to achieve an end of hostilities through peaceful means? As far as we can tell, not at this point," Putin continued, as translated in Russian media.

Putin on the Crimean Bridge attacks emphasized that the Ukrainians are attacking vital civilian instructure:

The president stated that he had deliberately ordered not to use the strategic link between the Russian peninsula and Krasnodar Region for any military logistics to ensure its status as a purely civiian infrastructure. Kiev insists that the bridge is a legitimate military target.

Putin then warned in follow-up: "We will not seek an agreement, we will respond to those strikes" - as Russian retaliation "will be far more painful than what the Kiev regime did to the bridge." Headline out of Russian state press:

For some of the latest that's been floated, but which has proven an automatic non-starter for Moscow:

Read our: Donbas For NATO? Zelensky Says Washington Just Floated A Swap That Crosses Putin's Reddest Line

Simply put, Russia is never going to let go of its captured eastern territories, and is demanding full political recognition of Russian sovereignty over them.

Ukraine's focus has remained to get the Europeans at the table, extending the trilateral talks format that was begun earlier this month in Abu Dhabi. Russia has warned that no, this won't happen and that the hawkish EU has nothing fruitful to offer.

But even as the EU is sidelined, Brussels is watching from afar as President Trump greats his Russian counterpart as "friend":

President Trump greeted Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “friend” Thursday, as the two arrived for a meeting in China.

“Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump is heard saying, after walking into a room with his Russian counterpart.

Heads exploding in Europe and among hawkis in Congress after this chummy greet in China...

All of this means Moscow still sees itself as in the driver's seat, and so is expected to set the parameters and agenda for further trilateral talks involving the US and Ukraine. Given the warm scenes out of China between Trump and Putin, it's likely finally dawning on Brussels that there's nothing European leaders can do about it.

items.title: Rebellion Against Jeffries Disintegrates In Landslide Speaker Nomination: Will The Same Happen With Schumer?
items.content_text:
Rebellion Against Jeffries Disintegrates In Landslide Speaker Nomination: Will The Same Happen With Schumer?

Two weeks of post-midterm histrionics about a rebellion against House Democratic Party leader Hakeem Jeffries evaporated on Wednesday, as the New Yorker won the House speaker nomination in a lopsided 251-11 vote. The outcome threw cold water on the party's progressive wing, which had branded Jeffries as just another establishmentarian who's all too willing to bend to the wishes of big business and keep on funding and arming the State of Israel. 

The nomination all but assures he will become the Speaker of the House on January 3, when the 120th Congress convenes and holds a vote. Forever enmeshed in identity-politics, major media outlets emphasized that he will be the first black speaker. In the run-up to Wedneday's vote, some of Jeffries' backers had implied that much of the opposition to his speakership sprang from racism, as demonstrated in this exchange on Jake Tapper's CNN show: 

The goofiness of that claim was brilliantly illuminated on Wednesday. Voting for the speaker nomination is conducted via secret ballots, but, of seven members-elect who've publicized their votes, six of them are non-white and four are black. That group of seven progressives issued a joint statement after the balloting. “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. They added that they've worked to "secure commitments" from Jeffries on those issues, but that "there is still work to be done" and that "our vote in caucus today was no." 

Last week, Jeffries was subjected to serial heckling when he spoke at the What's Next conference, where Democratic leaders, strategists, and newly elected lawmakers gathered to plan how to use the new majorities and how to position the party for 2028. "YOU'RE A F***ING LIAR!" one man yelled. His and other disruptive tirades accused Jeffries of "being in the pocket of corporations," "tak[ing] money from private equity" and "shaking hands with the Trump family." 

On Monday, California Democrat Ro Khanna said he would support Jeffries, but told Cenk Uyger that he was thus far disappointed that he and other were unable to secure commitments from Jeffries on two key demands: eliminating military aid to Israel, and killing NDAA Section 219, which, if enacted in the coming weeks, would integrate the United States and Israeli militaries.  

In other balloting for House Democratic leadership positions, Massachusetts Rep. Katherine Clark was chosen as Majority Leader, while California Rep. Pete Aguilar will be Majority Whip. California Rep. Ted Lieu will chair the Democratic Caucus. 

Now we'll have to wait to see whether the race for the Senate Majority Leader nomination ends in similarly anticlimactic fashion. In the upper chamber, New York's Chuck Schumer is squaring off against Maryland's Chris Van Hollen. According to a New York Times tracker of that contest, 16 Democrats have publicly said they'll vote for Schumer. Five have endorsed Van Hollen, and another five have called for "change." The remaining 29 have yet to voice their feelings. It will take 28 votes to win.
