Van Hollen flew to El Salvador last year to object to the deportation of Kilmar Ábrego García, while party leaders like Jeffries were encouraging Democrats to downplay Trump’s immigration abuses.

These are fundamentally different approaches to liberal/Democratic/anti-Trump politics. They should be debated openly and forcefully. I would love Van Hollen to win, but even if he loses, I’m thrilled he will have articulated an alternative to Schumer’s leadership. It would be great to see Ocasio-Cortez or someone with her ideology run for president, and why not a fighter in the mold of Pritzker too?

I suspect that many in the populist left and fighter camps are wary of entering battles that they will lose. The center-left is backed by the wealthiest and most famous Democrats and the most powerful media institutions. They will come out front most of the time. But the only contests you are guaranteed to lose are those that you don’t enter in the first place. The Sanders and Elizabeth Warren presidential campaigns transformed the Democratic Party and America, even though both lost. Mamdani, perhaps even more of a long shot in his mayoral run than Warren or Sanders were in seeking the presidency in 2020, won and has become one of the most influential politicians of this era.

So let’s have the fights. They don’t mean that Democrats are in disarray. They mean that Democrats are in democracy, where competing ideas, ideologies, and personalities should be welcomed and encouraged. May the best faction win.

items.title: How New York Failed Jordan Neely
items.content_text:
In January 2017, Jordan Neely checked in at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan. He was schizophrenic and addicted to the synthetic drug K2, and he didn’t have a place to live. Bellevue treated him for five weeks but couldn’t offer much long-term help. One professional wrote in Neely’s file that he ought to attend recovery meetings—“to identify at least 2 triggers for substance use,” as if the triggers weren’t already clear. Eventually the hospital turned him back out to the streets.

Several months later, Neely, who was 24, showed up at Mount Sinai Morningside. He’d been smoking K2 and sleeping at a Popeyes restaurant before he arrived. This was a brief visit—but in the fall he showed up there again, after a three-week stay in another facility. He said he was suicidal because had “nowhere to live and no girlfriend.” The hospital fed him dinner then discharged him.

Neely rounded out the year with two stays at Gracie Square Hospital on the Upper East Side. Again he told staffers he was suicidal because he was homeless and had no income. The hospital ultimately recommended (among other measures) that Neely “attend daily therapeutic groups,” hoping these would promote “stable mood, optimistic thinking and compliance with treatment.” Again it sent him “home.”

These experiences were typical of what Neely went through every year. And yet he managed to survive for six years longer. If his name is familiar, it’s because of the way he died. On a Saturday afternoon in 2023, he was pacing around on a subway car, ranting loudly. “I don’t care if I die,” one person remembered him saying. “I don’t care if you die. Kill me. Lock me up.” Daniel Penny, a fellow passenger who had been in the Marine Corps, decided Neely posed an imminent threat. Penny put him in a chokehold, wrestling him to the floor and not letting go for several minutes. By the time Penny released his grip, Neely’s pulse was faint, and he was soon declared dead.

Penny was indicted on a charge of manslaughter, and the case became a Rorschach test for how Americans thought about crime and mental illness in major cities. For some, it looked like a clear case of criminal homicide, in which a white man had strangled a Black man who was in crisis—while to others, Penny’s actions seemed justified amid rising fears of crime on the subways. (Ultimately, in December 2024, a Manhattan jury acquitted Penny.) This was a rare moment when conservatives blamed structural problems and deemphasized Penny’s personal responsibility. But most everyone agreed that in the months and years leading up to that incident, Neely deserved better treatment. Someone, or some institution, should have done more to help him.

In his new book, Man in the Mirror, the journalist Anand Giridharadas takes on the unwieldy story of Neely’s death and its aftermath. The book is at once an examination of the events that led to the killing, a study of the government policies that failed Neely, a narrative account of the trial, and a portrait of the divisions that have taken hold in American society. In its intensive reporting and its focus on the lives of normal people—from the streets of Manhattan to the suburbs of Long Island—it represents a turn for Giridharadas, who is best known for his 2018 bestseller Winners Take All, a polemic focused squarely on the rich and powerful (though his first two books were also traditional works of narrative journalism).

Most everyone agreed that in the months and years leading up to his death, Neely deserved better treatment. Someone, or some institution, should have done more to help him.

Ultimately Man in the Mirror ends up being too panoramic. Instead of tracking closely with Neely’s and Penny’s lives, the perspective shifts between dozens of characters, some of whom appear for just a few pages. Nor does Giridharadas make any explicit argument, though the narration often calls out for one. However, at its most illuminating, the book’s efforts to show the longer story of Neely’s life help restore a sense of Neely as an individual, far beyond the awful events of that day on the subway. It also gives glimpses, here and there, of what a better system—one that could have saved Neely’s life—might look like.


One of the most memorable sections in Man in the Mirror is a flashback to a morning in 2007 when Neely woke up alone. He was 14, two months away from finishing eighth grade. Normally his mother, Christie Neely, went into his bedroom and made sure he was ready to catch the bus at 7 a.m. He wondered if she was still asleep.

For two years, mother and son had been living in Bayonne, New Jersey. Their lives together had been rough but seemed to be on the upswing. Christie Neely had grown up in Washington Heights, where her father was a carpet cleaner. Jordan, her only child, was born in 1992. As of 2007, when she was in her mid-thirties, she had charges on her record for drug possession and prostitution, but she had turned her life around and found a steady job in telemarketing in Manhattan.

Shawn Southerland, her boyfriend, was awake that morning. Southerland had been part of the Neelys’ lives, off and on, since the early 2000s—but he and Christie fought constantly, and at one point she and Jordan had decamped for a domestic violence shelter. Now Southerland was living with them again.

Before Jordan Neely caught the bus, he wanted to say goodbye to his mother, but Southerland blocked him from the bedroom. Later that day, when Jordan got home from school, Southerland packed up all his belongings and left, saying he needed to go stay with a sick aunt. And in the evening, Christie Neely did not come home. Several days later, police found her body beside the Henry Hudson Parkway in the Bronx. It turned out Southerland had left her there after strangling her.

Christie’s death was understandably a shattering event for Jordan Neely. He did finish high school, with support from relatives, but he floundered after graduation. The one passion he latched onto was dancing like Michael Jackson as a “tribute artist.” Moses Harper, an older dancer who became Neely’s mentor, explains to Giridharadas that Neely wanted to be “active in his healing,” and dancing became a medium for that. However, Harper also counseled Neely that performing would never be enough to sustain him; he needed some kind of larger plan or vision for his life.

The advice never took. Neely drifted away from the group, and the last time Harper saw him—on a subway, in 2016—he was “visibly homeless.” Harper gave him her shirt and stuffed some money into his pocket. “When you’re ready to get clean,” she told him, “I got your back.”

But by this time, Neely was already cycling in and out of psychiatric wards. All told, from 2015, when he was 22, until his death eight years later, he was hospitalized at least 14 times. He was also arrested repeatedly, sometimes on violent charges.

Neely’s last chance to escape this cycle came in April 2023. Homeless outreach workers found him at the Coney Island subway station, drug-addled and with holes in his clothes. He exposed himself and urinated in front of the workers. They worried that he might hurt himself or someone else, so they consulted NYPD officers, who persuaded Neely to accept a shelter placement. The cops took him to a waiting van. But the driver, who worked on a contract with the city, refused to take Neely unless he had an escort. While the driver was arguing with the police, Neely wandered off.


As of that spring, Daniel Penny, who was 24, had been living in New York City for the better part of a year. He was taking architecture classes and teaching swimming lessons at a gym. Giridharadas, in the course of his reporting, visited West Islip, the Long Island suburb where Penny grew up. Over lunch, the editor of a local newspaper described the town as “the Long Island version of a flyover state.” Like much of Nassau County, it’s a haven for families who decided, at one point or another, to trade the excitement of city life for backyard barbecues and Little League games.

In Penny’s case, that choice was made a couple generations earlier. The high school he graduated from, West Islip High, is the same one his grandmother and his father attended. But he found the town stifling. When he joined the Marine Corps, immediately after high school, he did so “in search of adventure,” as he later said. He was inspired by Don Quixote—who, as Penny put it, left “his ‘normal’ life to pursue his dreams despite [being] called a madman.” Penny spent four years in the military, much of that time deployed on a ship in the Mediterranean, before returning to civilian life.

It was around 2:30 p.m. on May 1, a Saturday, when Penny and Neely found themselves on the same subway car. The story of their encounter is well known, and much of it was captured on a cell phone video that played countless times on broadcasts and in social media feeds.

Penny’s trial doesn’t begin until the last third of Man in the Mirror, but even so, it generates most of the book’s narrative momentum. Anyone who followed the news coverage will go in knowing the outcome: In December 2024, Penny was acquitted of criminally negligent homicide, after the jury deadlocked on a manslaughter charge. And yet Giridharadas still creates a sense of suspense. One reason is that we want to understand why the jurors voted the way they did.

One factor was that as of 2024, even seasoned New Yorkers felt that subway crime had gotten out of control (even though, by the numbers, it was at a historic low). For context, Penny’s trial wrapped up only five weeks after the 2024 presidential election, in which Donald Trump made surprising gains in New York City. There may have been a correlation. In the book’s jarring final scene, Penny is standing outside a bar, smoking, in the hours right after his acquittal. Numerous people who recognize him come up to thank him.

However, it’s likely that the biggest factor in Penny being freed was the jury selection. Months before the trial, the defense team hired a jury consultant—“one of the leading jury whisperers in the world,” per Giridharadas. She convened a focus group in downtown Manhattan, trying out several arguments to see how participants would react. One key takeaway was that Black people were far more likely than whites to think Penny was guilty. With that in mind, defense lawyers used almost all of their peremptory challenges to keep Black people from serving on the jury—and the judge upheld this arrangement. In a city that is 20 percent Black, only one Black person ended up serving on a jury of 12, and his answers during voir dire suggested that he had a problem with drug users.


Man in the Mirror is principally about two themes: first, the ways in which our society has failed people like Jordan Neely, the homeless and the mentally ill; and second, the polarization that has taken hold in our country. In a recent New York Times essay, Giridharadas brought these themes together in a pithy thesis statement. “A death on the subway that seemed to prove that Americans now inhabit perfectly sealed, irreconcilable moral universes,” he wrote, “actually revealed one of the last things we have in common—abandonment.”

But for whatever reason, Giridharadas doesn’t engage in this kind of interpretation in the book itself. There’s no thesis statement, and even teasing out the main themes requires some discernment on the reader’s part. Resisting interpretation was clearly a deliberate choice by Giridharadas, who is fabulously skilled at pressing arguments when he wants to.

Resisting interpretation was clearly a deliberate choice by Giridharadas, who is fabulously skilled at pressing arguments when he wants to.

The author has said he drew inspiration from two classic works of narrative journalism: Adrian Nicole LeBlanc’s Random Family, which was published in 2003, and Katherine Boo’s Behind the Beautiful Forevers, from 2012. Neither of those books makes an explicit argument, either; instead the takeaways emerge naturally from the storytelling. But that doesn’t happen as successfully in Man in the Mirror. The narration in this book is diffuse. We find ourselves inhabiting the perspectives of many different characters—from unhoused people to social workers, from defense lawyers to prosecutors. Giridharadas’s empathy is commendable, and there’s value in this kind of sweep, but ultimately the book fails to say enough about anything in particular.

It turns out that a fresh look at Neely’s death, and Penny’s trial, reveals little that wasn’t already expressed in the commentary at the time. We already know New York has a dire housing shortage, that the closure of America’s psychiatric hospitals in the 1960s and ’70s left a void in the infrastructure that has never been entirely filled, and that poor people are treated cruelly here—despite the best efforts of many activists, bureaucrats, and nonprofits. Nor is there anything novel about the notion that we’re polarized. The social ills reflected in this case are already all too familiar.

However, the book does have a scene, situated midway through, that points toward a possible solution for some of those problems. Giridharadas visits a facility in Midtown operated by the organization Fountain House. It’s a place where mentally ill people can go for therapy and other services—but also where they can find community and a sense of purpose. Together, the members run a café, an art studio and gallery, a newspaper, and a literary magazine (The Fountain Pen). They have a gardening unit and a research unit that produces reports on mental health. The list goes on.

One of the book’s heroes is Ashwin Vasan, who was the president and CEO of Fountain House before Mayor Eric Adams hired him as the city’s health commissioner. Throughout the book, Vasan tries to convince other policymakers that these “clubhouses” represent a solution hiding in plain sight. On the day of Giridharadas’s visit, an envoy from Joe Biden’s administration is also there for a tour. Vasan tries to persuade her that Fountain House’s model ought to be scaled up dramatically. But the organization’s loose, voluntaristic approach doesn’t square with the technocratic, data-driven methods she’s been trained in, and she’s visibly bored. The meeting amounts to nothing. “It was easier to count overdoses than the social contacts that might blunt the despair of addicts,” Giridharadas writes.

Admittedly, the notion that “community is the therapy”—the central idea behind these clubhouses—might sound a little misty-eyed and naïve. But it’s hard to dismiss the portrait Giridharadas presents of a young woman he meets at the facility. She tells him her mother had a breakdown when the woman was young, and she was later abused in foster care. By age 18, she was living in a shelter. In addition to cerebral palsy, she was diagnosed with major depressive disorder and PTSD. In other words, her background is remarkably similar to Neely’s. But as a young adult, she found her way to Fountain House—and through its education unit, she earned two bachelor’s degrees and a master’s. She now works as a “peer specialist,” helping other people navigate the mental health system. “When I’m here, I don’t remember that I have a mental illness, because here your focus isn’t your illness,” she says of the clubhouse. But in general, people on the outside “don’t consider, outside of the illness, how people live their lives. They only see when someone’s not doing well, and that’s all they can see.”

items.title: Trump Rages at Aides Over Losses as Even Podcast Bros Turn Against Him
items.content_text: Just after the election, Donald Trump promised to work with Democrats. But The Atlantic reports this remarkable tidbit: “As he watched television in the days that followed and called his outside advisers, he grew steadily angrier,” and he “needed someone to blame.” That fury helped drive him to promote Stephen Miller to chief of staff, per The Atlantic. In short: His rage led him to double down. This comes as many of the “podcast bros” are excoriating him over the midterms. Joe Rogan insisted Trump “lost most of the country” over mass deportations and war. Andrew Schulz tore into his broken promises as the “greatest failure” of any modern president. And Tim Dillon savaged his economy. We talked to New Republic staff writer Monica Potts, who’s been writing well about the failures of GOP economics. We discuss why Trump and MAGA can’t accept that their worldview spawned this electoral debacle, how Trumponomics sold young men a pack of economic lies, and how Democrats can step into the vacuum. Listen to this episode here. A transcript is here.

items.title: California Sues AI Giant Over Rogue Bot Activity
items.content_text:
California has sued OpenAI for allegedly endangering public safety by not appropriately safeguarding its artificial intelligence models.

The state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, cited a security breach in July, in which two OpenAI models broke out of their testing environment and hacked the platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said that the models broke out in order to try and cheat on a test, and they succeeded.

“Without proper safeguards and monitoring, these models pose a danger to anything connected to the internet,” Bonta said at a press conference Monday. “They can intrude into, degrade or shut down the services people rely on every day, including our power grids, our hospital systems, our financial institutions, and other critical infrastructure.”

The breach rattled the industry, prompting attempts to impose more safeguards on AI. A number of Democrats have proposed bills to regulate AI, including Ro Khanna and Lori Trahan. OpenAI isn’t the only company that’s had models go rogue: Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also disclosed similar breaches. However, OpenAI is the first to be sued by California in relation to the security incidents.

“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” Open AI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said in a statement. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity.”

OpenAI is facing a number of other lawsuits, including from Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier alleging that OpenAI knowingly released an unsafe product, and from individuals alleging that ChatGPT led users to commit suicide.

items.title: Team Trump Actually Made the FAA Disaster Way Worse Than Necessary
items.content_text:
Air traffic controllers are saying that there was no need for the Trump administration to issue the hourslong nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights and cost the economy billions of dollars.

During an appearance on MS NOW’s The Assignment Sunday, The Washington Examiner’s Anna Giaritelli said she’d spoken with multiple air traffic controllers who believed that the nationwide ground stop on Friday was entirely unnecessary.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has repeatedly blamed the cascading telecommunications outage on outdated air traffic control systems, turning the crisis into a plea to receive additional funding.

In July 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion in order to overhaul the air traffic control system. So far, the FAA has only used a small portion of those funds across more than 10,000 projects nationwide. But in August 2026, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Giaritelli that the agency needed an additional $19 billion to complete the project. By October, that number rose to $30 billion. As of this week, the agency is asking for an additional $50 billion.

Giaritelli claimed that she’d been overwhelmed with messages from air traffic controllers who “don’t believe” Duffy’s explanations.

“There’s already protocols in place for whether FAA or contractors are making changes to the system. They do that in the middle of the week, in the middle of the night when there are no flights happening,” she said.

Duffy claimed that the outage began during a routine router upgrade at a remote radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris contract workers were updating a copper wire–based system with fiber optic cable. There was also a second, unrelated issue at a radar facility in Texas. But Giaritelli said she’d spoken with air traffic controllers and technicians across the country who reported experiencing other technical issues hours before the ground stop was announced.

FAA workers also didn’t understand how the kind of upgrade that had supposedly caused the outage could result in a nationwide issue, Giaritelli said. Even Duffy has admitted that the agency hadn’t anticipated that the upgrade could “take down the system.”

The reason for the outage is still being investigated. The FBI announced Monday that the agency had taken possession of the router and other equipment that was involved in the outage.

items.title: Vance Flails While Defending Grounded Flights to Fox News
items.content_text:
Vice President JD Vance blamed Congress for Friday’s nationwide flight stoppage, shifting responsibility away from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s Federal Aviation Administration. But Fox News wasn’t buying it.

“We’re dealing with fifty-year-old technology. It works most of the time,” Vance told Laura Ingraham in an interview that will air Monday night. “Secretary Duffy has done an amazing job at this—sometimes you have to work on a patchwork of solutions to keep a fifty-year-old system up and running. Why do we have a fifty-year-old system in the first place?”

“Well, you guys have been in charge for the last two years. Why hasn’t it gotten fixed?” Ingraham replied.

“Well, a lot of the stuff that needed to get fixed, we have been working on and have been patching that stuff, Laura. But in terms of rebuilding the infrastructure using twenty-first-century technology, that is something that Congress needs to reinvest, give us the resources to do,” Vance replied.

Vance’s response follows the same lack of accountability that Trump and Duffy took Monday. Trump has been in power not just the past two years, but six out of the past 10 years. Surely this issue could have been addressed then and averted the sudden cancellation of thousands of flights on Friday. And why bring up Congress when the GOP has controlled it for the past two years?

“Every single time Vance is in the hot seat he always does this bizarre thing where he acts like he’s just a Regular Guy, as powerless as you are,” journalist Pedro L. Gonzalez wrote online. “Best part is he and his allies probably think this is a brilliant rhetorical move, nobody will notice that he’s the Vice President.”

items.title: The MAGA Manosphere Is Breaking Apart
items.content_text:
After Donald Trump won a second term, the Democrats feared they had lost the majority of young men for good. According to Tufts polling, Trump won 56 percent of the young male vote. Political observers blamed the “manosphere,” a loose conglomerate of podcasters, comedians, and social media influencers who built large audiences with politically incorrect humor and a promise of masculine camaraderie. It seemed that, just as young women were more liberal than ever, young men were running in the other direction, becoming not just conservative but, in many cases, radicalized.

When pastor Joel Webbon first announced the “Christ Is King: America After Trump” conference in May, he undoubtedly hoped to build on this rightward surge among young men to create a far-right movement that could outlast Trump. “We’re going to win in the long run,” he said at the time. The speaker list for the conference—hosted last week by the Texas-based NXR Studios, which is short for “New Christian Right”—included unapologetic white nationalist Nick Fuentes and failed Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, both of whom have grown large audiences of young men with shock-value tactics like regularly using racial slurs and calling women “whores.” Even the name of the conference is a reference to an antisemitic dog whistle popular in right-wing spaces online.

Webbon and his guests clearly hoped to harness this youthful enthusiasm for edgy rhetoric toward fascistic goals like ending women’s rights and creating a white country through mass deportations—which, a few months ago, did not seem like a pie-in-the-sky goal. As Senator Ted Cruz and other Republican leaders complained to The Wall Street Journal in October, “Groypers”—the nickname given to young men who have these extremist views—dominate the ranks of young Republicans. Vice President JD Vance seems to have pinned his presidential hopes on them, making sure to be seen defending young Republicans caught praising Hitler or using the n-word.

But that was all before a midterm election where young male voters swung nearly 40 points to the left, which cast a pall over the poorly timed “Christ Is King” conference. An event that was supposed to launch a youthful, ultraradical MAGA movement turned out to be yet another sign that MAGA is dying.

Webbon, Fuentes, and other speakers at the conference did try mightily to keep up claims that they are at the forefront of an authoritarian revolution. Webbon promised a new America where “men are doing what God designed them to do and women [are] cheerful and happy in the home.” Fishback invited the audience to “burn down a Planned Parenthood,” calling it the “righteous thing to do.” Talk-show host Alex Jones declared, “We’re here tonight because we know that Christianity and the West and white people are under attack,” but promised they would not “surrender,” and instead fight “total war.”

Webbon “thinks he’ll be able to launch a competitor to Turning Point USA,” argued journalist Anna Merlan, who attended the conference, on Bluesky. But that seemed a harder sell than ever. After all, the conference was in Texas, which had just turned bright blue after decades of seemingly permanent Republican rule. According to CNN, the conference turnout was only in the hundreds, despite the presence of Fuentes, whose podcast gets hundreds of thousands of views per episode.

Fuentes tried to reassure the audience. “When we talk about ’26, that’s not us,” he said in his speech. “We did not lose. It was the Republican Party that lost,” he continued, arguing that MAGA’s ultimate victories would come from running even further to the right than Trump, toward even more open racism and misogyny.

Likelier, the opposite is true: The loud radicalism of figures like Fuentes, Webbon, and others contributed to the blue wave. When Trump was out of power, it was easy for voters, especially young male voters, to write off the extremist rhetoric of the manosphere as jokes or devil’s advocacy, meant to shock the liberals and titillate their audiences. Now that Trump is in office and Immigration and Customs Enforcement is grabbing people off the street, it’s a lot harder to see this all as just talk.

Some of the more secular voices in the manosphere seem to realize this and are backpedaling away from MAGA. Joe Rogan, who not only endorsed Trump but regularly features some of the more extremist figures of the MAGA movement on his show, admitted last week that Trump lost “the podcast bros,” along with the rest of the country. There is a real sense that the fever is breaking. It may have been daring and cool to be MAGA in 2024, but it’s now looking very uncool indeed.

At the “Christ Is King” conference, though, the views were as radical as ever. Most of these influencers have little choice. Someone like Rogan can pivot to a more moderate-sounding set of views because his podcast is about all sorts of topics, not just politics. But people like Webbon and Fuentes can only get attention through political shock value. They built their audiences in no small part on curiosity about what crazy things they may say next. If they stop doing that, they really have nothing left to offer.

At one point, Fuentes seemed to acknowledge that democracy simply was not going to be their path to victory, instead arguing that “a small group of fanatics, zealots, the martyrs, the people that are willing to die for what they believe in” would have to bring his vision into being. These frightening words thrilled the audience, but ultimately it’s a sign of a losing movement. Fuentes and his followers are escaping into fantasy, rather than admitting defeat.

The conference was a microcosm of the larger dilemma facing the MAGA movement in Trump’s second term. The base is, in a very real sense, addicted to extremist rhetoric. To keep the high going, it needs ever uglier content, both from influencers using racial slurs and from the administration itself, pumping out videos of immigrants getting arrested in violent and humiliating fashion. But the more that MAGA leaders indulge the hardcore base’s sadistic whims, the more they turn off others who might have right-wing inclinations, but only to a point.

Webbon was right that the “Christ Is King” conference represents the post-Trump phase of MAGA, but not in the way he envisioned. He pictured a new front of radicalized young men who would take Trumpism to the next level. Instead, his conference was populated by the dwindling number of social malcontents rallying around a dying cause. No doubt the far far right will stick around for a while, saying ever more vile things online in an effort to troll liberals and get attention. But the louder they get, the fewer young men seem interested in listening.

items.title: Stephen Miller’s Chilling Comment to RFK Jr. Exposed as Measles Surges
items.content_text:
White House chief of staff Stephen Miller might be about to turbocharge Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s anti-vax agenda.

The health secretary revealed last week that Miller had recently enthusiastically rubber-stamped Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement while the two shared a meal at Miller’s home.

“During that dinner, [Miller] said to me, ‘I’m the only one in the administration who’s more radical than you are on MAHA,’” Kennedy said at an event hosted by the advocacy group MAHA Action. Kennedy recalled that Miller said he wanted to make MAHA his “top priority,” effectively shelving the immigration fixation Miller has carried since he entered office.

Miller and his wife are, like Kennedy, against inoculations. Katie Miller told her podcast listeners earlier this year that she considers her youngest, entirely unvaccinated child to be her “healthiest.” Months later in August, Miller commended Donald Trump for signing an executive order to disrupt the childhood vaccine schedule and separate the trifold measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine.

“The fact that you had the courage to push this forward knowing the unfair criticisms from some in the establishment and to give the chance for [Kennedy], who spent decades representing parents, to stand here today, it’s such a profound moment,” Miller said at the time.

Meanwhile, the anti-vax crusade has resulted in nothing other than unnecessary and completely preventable deaths. The U.S. is currently seeing an unprecedented surge in measles. Growing distrust of modern medicine and falling vaccination rates, which have reliably abated the disease since 1963, resulted in the U.S. losing its measles elimination status this month, marking the first time in 26 years that the country has failed to contain the disease.

As a result, doctors across the country are being forced to confront a spate of symptoms that they’ve either never encountered before (due to measles’ long-standing eradication status) or haven’t confronted in decades, according to The Washington Post.

“There is a tremendous amount of what I would describe as learning on the fly,” John Goldman, an epidemiologist at UPMC Harrisburg, told the Post on Saturday.

items.title: DOJ Threatens Elizabeth Warren Over Trump Investigations
items.content_text:
The Department of Justice sent Senator Elizabeth Warren a warning letter, saying that she could face “significant legal consequences” if she doesn’t preserve records related to investigations into President Donald Trump, The Guardian reported.

The letter, sent by U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz, said that Warren appeared “eager to wield [her] future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates.” Warren is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee next year, and recently signaled that she will begin investigating people within the Trump administration for corruption.

She’s not the only Democrat who’s received a warning from the DOJ: Representative Robert Garcia, the next chair of the House Oversight Committee, was told last week that the administration was “monitoring” Democrats’ potential investigations, and that some of the inquiries could constitute criminal behavior.

Senator Richard Blumenthal was also threatened via a similar letter from Reitz for reaching out to more than a dozen undisclosed donors to the White House ballroom.

The threat related to Warren preserving records mirrors Warren’s own requests to top Trump fundraiser Meredith O’Rourke, asking that she preserve documents related to the ballroom funding. But Warren and other congressional Democrats have good reason to follow the money: Donors to Trump’s ballroom have already begun to cash in, with 14 donors raking in more than $50 billion in government contracts so far.

items.title: Howard Lutnick Keeps Changing AI Rules to Help His Business
items.content_text:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick may have reined in rules on AI chips to the benefit of his family’s business. 

A client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm Lutnick handed off to his sons when he joined President Donald Trump’s Cabinet, owns A201, a new data center in Malaysia that is set to open next year, The New York Times reported Monday. 

The data center, owned by Singaporean firm Bitdeer, is poised to sell Nvidia chips to a Chinese tech giant, sidestepping U.S. rules that ban the sales of advanced U.S. chips to China. Cantor Fitzgerald served as a sales agent for a Bitdeer equity offering of up to $1 billion, and assisted the company with arranging a stock offering of up to $250 million. Cantor Fitzgerald also has business ties to several data center companies in Southeast Asia. 

The Trump administration has been embroiled in debate on how much the government should regulate the sale of AI chips to foreign countries, with Lutnick leading the effort to scale back U.S. oversight. As Commerce secretary, he has championed Nvidia, offering the company unprecedented access to rulemaking and refusing to crack down on foreign chip sales. Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang was ousted from the company last week after revelations that he’d had multiple affairs, one of them with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, whose company Megaspeed is being investigated for illegally selling Nvidia’s chips.

There is no evidence that Cantor’s investments influenced Lutnick’s decisions, but the company’s business ties to data centers present yet another obvious conflict of interest for the embattled commerce secretary.

items.title: Yet Another System Crashes in Trump’s America
items.content_text:
Multiple major banks are experiencing widespread outages Monday afternoon, leaving thousands of people unable to fully access their online financial services.

Bank of America, Chase, J.P. Morgan, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, and Zelle all experienced a high rate of reported outages, with Chase reporting 3,300 alone.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a spokesperson for Chase said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

While the impacts of this outage still remain to be seen, it comes just four days after a massive Microsoft service outage and just two days after a nationwide flight stoppage. From messaging your coworkers, to catching your flight, to logging into your bank, the past few days have been very rough for technology in President Trump’s America. Although he’d probably blame former President Joe Biden for that.

items.title: Stephen Miller Is Already Planning For After Trump
items.content_text:
Marco Rubio and Stephen Miller have reportedly become much closer in the second Trump administration, reports The Wall Street Journal. Together, the duo is one of the most powerful influences on policy in Washington.

Now that Miller has been made White House chief of staff, he and Rubio will have even more sway over the president. Miller’s xenophobic views and extreme approach to immigration enforcement certainly didn’t help Republicans in the midterms, but despite that, President Donald Trump seems to be doubling down on Miller’s brutal, racist tactics.

Rubio, meanwhile, has a lot of influence in his dual role as secretary of state and national security adviser, and knows how to sell potentially controversial policies. Together, the two men have cooked up some of the most brazen foreign policy moves of the last two years: the plan to seize Greenland, the likely illegal deadly boat strikes, and the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, according to the Journal.

For anyone who knows Rubio and Miller’s history, their close relationship may come as a surprise: The two initially butted heads when Rubio was working on immigration reform and Miller was an adviser to Republican Senator Jeff Sessions. Miller reportedly worked fiercely to undermine Rubio, and called him an “extremist who wants unlimited immigration.”

However, during the second Trump administration, Rubio has reportedly done all he can to enforce Miller’s hardline immigration crackdown, and personally flew to El Salvador to negotiate a deal to send U.S. deportees to the country’s megaprison, where many have suffered abuse.

Maybe Miller is angling for a position in a future Rubio presidency, or maybe he’s just smitten by Rubio’s commitment to mass deportation, but the two men are closer than ever: Miller’s wife refers to them as “besties,” and the pair even spend family gatherings together.

items.title: Trump Admin Blames Everyone But Themselves for Grounded Flights
items.content_text:
The Trump administration is blaming everyone but itself for the nationwide flight stoppage that the Federal Aviation Administration instituted on Friday.

“The FAA administrator apologized to the American people during the news conference you held yesterday,” NBC’s Kristen Welker asked Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Monday morning. “Do you feel you also owe an apology to the American people? This happened on your watch.”

“It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or the [Department of Transportation] in decades. And I’m proud of the work we’re doing, the attention we’re bringing to this issue,” Duffy replied. “But I can’t apologize for what was passed off to us. And I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats because it’s all of them! It goes back 25, 30 years of a lack of investment … waving the flag to say, ‘Hey, this is a problem, let’s fix it.’ Why they didn’t do that, I don’t know.”

“They gave me a system that needs to be fixed. And President Trump and I are gonna fix it. I’m well on my way, but I need more money to do it,” he continued.

Thousands of flights were cancelled over the weekend due to the Trump administration’s nationwide grounding, leaving countless Americans stranded and deeply inconvenienced. The administration has attributed the stoppage to faulty copper wiring and a router malfunction in Arkansas, denying reports that it had anything to do with the massive artificial intelligence systems overhaul the FAA performed just a day before. Regardless, for Duffy to refuse to apologize to them—dumping the issue on previous administrations—is weak and uncompelling, especially given that this was the first nationwide ground stop in years.

President Trump wasn’t keen on apologizing either.

“How much responsibility do you take for the ground stop on Friday given that you’re the president?” a reporter asked Trump on the White House lawn Monday.

“I don’t take any responsibility,” he replied. “Everybody was safe, nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing. The only responsibility should be for 40 years they should’ve done this.”

He blamed the Biden administration more explicitly over the weekend.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began,” he wrote Sunday on Truth Social. “We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST! Our FAA is doing a great job, and is ready to go.” On Monday, he called a Black female reporter a “loser” for even asking about it.

items.title: Ousted Republican Rep. Plots How to Carpetbag His Way Back to Congress
items.content_text:
Some Republicans just don’t understand the word no.

Representative Gabe Evans lost to Democrat Manny Rutinel by double digits on Election Day, marking a drastic political shift in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, which suddenly flipped from red to blue.

But despite the will of the American people, Evans is not ready to lose his grip on power. The MAGA politico announced Monday that he’s going to run for Congress again in 2028, albeit in a different district.

“I know what it means to live rurally and depend on water, energy, and agriculture, because that’s how three generations of my family have lived in Douglas, Elbert, and Weld counties,” Evans said in a statement on Facebook. “Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls’ sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable.”

The Fort Lupton resident also suggested that the people of Colorado’s 4th district—which constitutes the Centennial State’s most conservative region—were at risk of losing their values to Democratic Socialists.

“The people of the 4th District grow our food, produce our energy, work in defense, aerospace, healthcare, and so many other sectors. They raise their families on values that Democrat Socialists and their allies keep trying to regulate out of existence. They deserve a representative with deep roots in the community who shows up for them, not one who answers to the coastal donors who just bought this seat,” Evans wrote, apparently referring to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, who bested Representative Lauren Boebert earlier this month.

(Interestingly enough, Boebert herself switched districts in 2023 after a close race in order to ensure herself an easier return to Congress. Although she won in 2024, she lost this time around in yet another stunning Democratic flip.)

The unusually early announcement will give Evans a remarkable head start in the 2028 race, entering the new year with $300,000 in campaign funds and regional name recognition that will make it difficult for new candidates to compete, according to the Colorado Sun.

But the region’s incoming lawmaker is ignoring the noise.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted five times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher wrote in a statement obtained by Colorado Public Radio’s Caitlyn Kim. “While Gabe Evans focuses on finding his way back to Washington, Eileen is focused on making Washington deliver for the people of Colorado’s 4th District.”

items.title: Trump Issues Crazed Threat to RNC Over Post-Election Rebellion
items.content_text:
President Donald Trump is threatening to turn the lights off at the Republican National Committee if it doesn’t reelect his handpicked chairman.

Trump and his administration officials were left fuming after RNC co-chair KC Crosbie launched a surprise bid to challenge chair Joe Gruters. Now a small, yet growing, group is backing a plan to depose the president’s handpicked party chairman, the Associated Press reported Sunday.

Just two days after the midterm elections, Crosbie announced her candidacy in a letter to the RNC’s 168 members. She questioned whether Republicans had done enough to address voter concerns to avoid the sweeping party losses. “Tuesday’s results were a serious setback,” she wrote. “We owe ourselves an honest account of why.”

The White House did not take kindly to the first major challenge to Trump’s authority within the Republican Party ranks. “The White House was blindsided by KC’s bid for RNC Chair and people are infuriated that she did not give anybody a courtesy call,” an administration official told Axios.

During a meeting in the White House on November 6, Trump warned that if Crosbie was crowned, he’d cut the financial cord. Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and other administration and Cabinet officials would no longer be permitted to appear at fundraising events. Trump would also bar the RNC from using his likeness and signature as part of fundraising efforts.

The RNC leadership election is expected to be held in January at the committee’s winter meeting in Arizona.

items.title: “Losers Like You”: Trump Tears Into Black Woman Reporter Over FAA
items.content_text:
The president was sent over the edge Monday by a simple question about the FAA’s ground stop, resulting in a lengthy tirade and a series of demeaning remarks against an inquiring Black woman reporter.

“Mr. President, what do you say to critics who say you were too focused on D.C. construction projects while our airline systems were crumbling, given the fact that Republicans have been in control?” NBC News White House Correspondent Yamiche Alcindor asked Donald Trump as he departed the White House for a trip to Asia.

But Trump was apparently uninterested in acknowledging the multibillion-dollar national airline crisis spurred by his administration on Friday, which required practically every plane in U.S. airspace to cut short its route and land at the nearest airport.

Instead, the president took the opportunity to exalt his White House renovations for the umpteenth time, all while disparaging Alcindor as “pathetic” and a “loser” for daring to question his vanity projects. When Alcindor attempted to ask a follow-up question, Trump shot her down.

“You’re so pathetic,” he fumed. “This doesn’t cost money. This is peanuts. I pay for it. This doesn’t cost money. This is called talent. You don’t have talent. You don’t know what a broken column is. When you see a broken column you don’t notice. But when other leaders of state and other people come here—the White House was in terrible condition. Now it’s in beautiful condition.”

“Cost me very little money to do it. I spent very little time to do it, and losers like you say, ‘Why are you focused on the White House?’ Because the White House is a symbol of our country, and the White House should look like that,” Trump said, extending his arm to gesture to the executive mansion behind him.

The Trump administration blamed the rare nationwide ground stop on faulty copper wiring and a bum router located in Arkansas. Senior officials denied that the rapid expansion of the agency’s artificial intelligence tools—which were rolled out the day prior—had anything to do with the critical failure.

items.title: Why the Heck Is Pete Hegseth’s Wife Making Decisions at the Pentagon?
items.content_text:
Jennifer Hegseth is producing her husband as if he’s on a Fox News show.

While Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has pushed America’s military to reject individualism, he and his wife have been busy gussying up at the Pentagon, demanding a makeup studio for his various speaking engagements, Hegseth’s former spokesman John Ullyot told The Daily Beast podcast on Saturday.

“He’s very image-conscious. That’s why he’ll have those pocket squares; he wears this sort of light blue suit with the flag pocket squares.... He’s very built on his image, and that probably helped him move up the ranks [at Fox News],” Ullyot shared on the podcast, harkening back to Hegesth’s years as an on-air anchor at the conservative media behemoth.

Jennifer and her “best friend,” another former Fox News producer, have reportedly been lending an assist, according to Ullyot. For instance, it was Jennifer’s friend who first pitched the concept of adding a makeup studio to Hegseth’s quarters.

“She came to me and said, ‘Hey, we need to, Pete expects to have a makeup studio if he’s going to be talking to the media,’ and I said that was kind of weird. I’ve never known a secretary of Defense to install a makeup studio, and I just thought that was crazy,” Ullyot told the podcast.

“It’s very strange,” he continued. “It’s contradictory because he talks about how he’s all about lethality and getting rid of wokeness, and now he wants to install a makeup studio in the office of the Pentagon. No Defense secretary had ever done that, but that shows how image-conscious he was.”

Ullyot rejected the studio request three times, arguing that the department lacked the budget to do so, but it was eventually installed after he was asked to resign in April 2025. “Ironically, Pete Hegseth has used that briefing room less than probably any secretary in history because he ... has a very adversarial approach with the press, kicked them out of the building, literally,” Ullyot added.

The ousted spokesman has been a vocal critic of Hegseth’s reign since he left, skewering the Defense secretary in broadcast and print. On Saturday, Ullyot told MS NOW that Hegesth was so “unfit” for the job that he should never have accepted Donald Trump’s offer in the first place.

“You’d get off the stage if you were truly loyal to President Donald Trump,” Ullyot told the network. “I’m saying that loyalty would require him—if he really does think that he’s serving the president well—well, you’d serve the president best if you got off the stage.”

items.title: Surprise! You’re Never Seeing a Dollar From Trump’s Tariff Refunds
items.content_text:
Wealthy corporations are using their hundreds of millions of dollars in tariff refunds to enrich themselves instead of returning it to the consumers who actually footed the bill.

Companies like Black & Decker, TJ Maxx, Marshalls, and Titleist all received massive refunds after the Supreme Court struck down President Trump’s retaliatory “Liberation Day” global tariffs, collectively receiving about $170 billion. New reporting from ProPublica shows that instead of returning that wealth back to the consumers who were hit with rising prices, they’ll be sending that cash to their own executives for bonuses—even as Trump’s tariffs cost the average household around $1,000 last year.

Rewarding already well-off executives for a failed government policy that hurt consumers more than it hurt their companies is plainly unjust—so much so that some of the companies that received refunds, like Black & Decker ($298 million) are being sued to force them to pay out the refund to consumers. It’s unlikely that the suit will be successful.

“The Republican economy in a nutshell: higher prices, fewer jobs for working people and big bonuses and stock buybacks for Republican billionaire donors,” Wisconsin Representative Gwen Moore wrote on Monday.

The Trump administration has had trouble even admitting that tariffs are a tax on the consumer, and President Trump himself encouraged companies like Walmart to “eat the costs” of the tariffs without charging consumers more. Now those companies are rewarding the executives who suffered least. This is your money, not theirs.

“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” Syracuse corporate law professor Gregory Germain told ProPublica. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.… It wasn’t the executive that triggered that extra profit, so why should their compensation go up?”

items.title: Here’s What Trump Was Doing While the FAA Imploded
items.content_text:
What was President Donald Trump doing during his administration’s massive screwup that halted air travel nationwide and sparked panic over cyberattacks?

Trump spent his Friday evening huddled in the Oval Office with his buddy, actor Jon Voight, two people familiar with the meeting told The Atlantic. Then Trump called a series of powerful figures in Hollywood to discuss legislation intended to revitalize the entertainment industry. One of the players the president phoned asked if his attention would be better spent on the major meltdown at the Federal Aviation Administration.

Shortly after those calls, Trump posted on Truth Social about the “unbelievable” popularity of his bipartisan effort to bring entertainment jobs back to the United States. He did not, however, address the nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights and cost the economy billions of dollars until Sunday.

When Trump did eventually address the crisis, it was to shift blame. “The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began,” he wrote on Truth Social Sunday, begging a (still Republican controlled) Congress to direct more funding to air traffic control.

Trump’s level of distraction has never been more obvious. Amid a national crisis, the president was too busy palling around with a celebrity to do anything. He then spent the whole weekend posting artificial intelligence–generated slop addressing public perception of the Iran war, the midterm losses, and his White House renovation projects.

items.title: The Multimillion-Dollar Reason Trump Is Still Backing Nvidia
items.content_text:
Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang was ousted from the company last week after revelations that he’d had multiple affairs, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy.

But despite the obvious threat to national security, President Donald Trump says he “wouldn’t mind” if Huang were reinstated. “I think he learned a big lesson,” the president said.

Why is Trump so keen on Huang? Perhaps because he has money on the line: Trump’s stake in Nvidia swelled to as much as $62 million by the end of August, according to The Washington Post.

This is a big change from the end of 2024, when the president only had somewhere between $615,000 to $1.3 million in Nvidia shares. And the real number could be even bigger, as Nvidia’s share price rose between the end of 2025 and the end of August, partially due to its ability to sell some of its chips to China—which the president permitted.

According to the White House, the president does not control his own stock portfolio. His assets are in a trust managed by his children, and his investment decisions are made by third-party financial institutions. Nvidia is a big chunk of most investment indexes, so it follows that Nvidia would be a big chunk of Trump’s investments as well.

Trump and Huang have enjoyed a close relationship over the past couple of years, with Huang flying in Air Force One and meeting the president at Mar-a-Lago to urge him to allow Nvidia access to profitable Chinese markets.

And Trump doesn’t seem to mind Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer, Megaspeed. U.S. officials suspect that Huang is a spy for China, but Trump doesn’t seem convinced: “I don’t know that she was a spy at all,” he said.

items.title: Trump Goes on Weird AI Posting Spree Instead of Talking About FAA
items.content_text:
Donald Trump was once again glued to his phone this weekend—but not in any way that could have assisted the public in navigating his administration’s massive Federal Aviation Administration screwup.

The president has posted numerous artificial intelligence–generated clips to his Truth Social accounts since Friday, apparently more fixated on the public perception of the Iran war, the midterm losses, and his White House renovation projects than the nationwide plane ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights and cost the economy billions of dollars.

One Sunday post depicted rows of sloppily generated Air Force troops kneeling and praying on a nondescript tarmac beside a pair of Boeing C-17 Globemaster III military transport aircraft.

Hours earlier, Trump recirculated AI-generated images of Defense Secretary Markwayne Mullin, though that, too, had little to do with the airline industry disaster. Instead, Trump shared fake images of himself holding Mullin’s 15-year-old son Jim, and more fake images of Mullin crying, alongside a story that recounted a story Mullin told during his Senate confirmation hearing in March about his son’s brain injury.

By Monday morning, the president could not offer a great explanation as to why he was so disinterested in the public emergency.

“What do you say to critics who say you are too focused on D.C. construction projects while our airlines are crumbling? Given the fact that Republicans have been in control?” one journalist pressed Trump outside the White House.

“Well, if you take a look at the White House, it’s flawless,” Trump said. “You never notice broken windows, obviously when you come, I don’t know.”

Trump then claimed that the White House had 18 broken windows before he began the renovations, and that plaster was falling off the exterior walls.

“It was an embarrassment, and you know it took me 10 minutes a day, because I know great construction people and I know people that can put it back. So the White House is in beautiful shape,” Trump said, briefly reorienting the conversation to the helipad he constructed in time for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival in September.

But as the journalist attempted to push Trump on the FAA issue, the president snapped. “Listen to me,” Trump seethed.

“It’s gotten great reviews. And nicest of all will be the ballroom, which people are saying fits like a glove. For 150 years, people have wanted it,” Trump insisted, adding that the “stone was badly broken.”

It was clear that the line of questioning about the FAA was getting on his nerves, as Trump derided the querying reporter as “pathetic.”

“I have a responsibility to make sure that the symbol of our country is in decent shape,” Trump said through his teeth.

“The White House was in terrible condition, now it’s in great condition,” he continued. “And losers like you come out and say, ‘Why are you focused on the White House?’ Because the White House is a symbol of our country.”

The Trump administration blamed the rare nationwide ground stop on faulty copper wiring and a bum router located in Arkansas. Senior officials denied that the rapid expansion of the agency’s AI tools—which were rolled out the day prior—had anything to do with the critical failure.

items.title: Pentagon Scrambles After Hegseth Accused of Ignoring Key Iran Intel
items.content_text:
The Pentagon is scrambling after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was accused of ignoring crucial warnings that led to the deaths of six U.S. military service members. 

Speaking on CBS News’s 60 Minutes Sunday, Major Stephen Ramsbottom, who survived the deadly attack on a U.S. base at Shuaiba port in Kuwait, accused military leadership of ignoring warnings that the base was not fortified for aerial attacks.

“It was, some people have phrased it as a trailer park,” Ramsbottom said. “The protection that was there was to stop car bombs and threats like that. There was nothing there designed to protect from an aerial attack.”

Ramsbottom claimed he repeatedly raised concerns about the safety of the military’s makeshift tactical operations center at Shuaiba port, but was told that the service members stationed there didn’t have to worry about protection. 

“I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself—all the way down to my level,” Ramsbottom said. He has filed a whistleblower complaint with the House and Senate.

Meanwhile, The Atlantic reported Sunday that a group of senior American military officers claim that U.S. military leadership ignored repeated warnings about a drone attack on that same U.S. base. Several of the officers who attempted to sound the alarm on the attacks have since been fired or forced into early retirement. 

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told The Atlantic that it was “disgusting” to suggest that the U.S. military was “unprepared” for the attack. 

“Central Command established the most extensive air defense umbrella in the world over the Middle East,” Parnell said in a statement to the publication. “Make no mistake: The U.S. military has the best offensive and defensive capabilities of any nation on Earth, and we always protect our bases and our people.”

In a post on Truth Social Monday, Trump lashed out at the “new people running” 60 Minutes, claiming that the drone attack at Shuaiba port was one of only two successful Iranian drone attacks. 

The Pentagon has consistently downplayed the severity of the strike. U.S. Central Command initially claimed that only five service members had been seriously wounded, but in reality, 30 people were wounded. The day after the attack happened, Hegseth called the strike “a squirter,” and later complained that reporting on the troops killed was a ploy to make the president look bad.  

Not only did the DOD apparently fail to provide the personnel stationed there with the necessary tools to defend themselves, but multiple service members who were injured in the attack say their government also neglected them in the aftermath.

items.title: Trump Demands More Money to Fix Flight Issues
items.content_text:
Artificial intelligence was not to blame for the nationwide grounding of airplanes, says the Federal Aviation Administration.

Instead, government officials say that a router issue was at fault: Problems during a routine router upgrade in Arkansas caused it to ping the FAA’s communications network hundreds of times per second, overwhelming the system and causing difficulties with air traffic communications.

However, not everyone buys the FAA’s explanation. Robert W. Mann Jr., the founder of an airline analysis and consulting firm, told The New York Times, “The idea that you would have a single router take down a national network is just not plausible.”

The timing of the ground stop also came conveniently close to the FAA’s rollout of a new AI system, SMART, an $875 million setup that officials say centralizes data on weather, flight paths, and staffing to help specialists find and fix problems in the sky. SMART was launched nationwide on November 10, three days before flights were grounded across the country.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday that there’s no indication that the new AI system was related to the ground stop, as did the startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence.

House Democrats are raising concerns about safety, and asked to audit the SMART system last month.

“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” Democrats on the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure said in an October 13 letter. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”

Meanwhile, the Trump administration is asking for more funding for the FAA, blaming this failure on old equipment.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that $50 billion is needed to upgrade the FAA’s network, but billions have already been spent: President Joe Biden awarded $25 billion over five years as part of a larger infrastructure bill, and $12.5 billion was approved in 2025 to modernize the FAA’s air traffic system.

President Donald Trump finally spoke up about the situation on Sunday morning, two days after the planes were grounded, advocating for further funding.

“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!”

items.title: Trump Still Crashing Out Over Midterm Elections
items.content_text:
President Trump is still whining about his poor midterm election results, posting a clip of a withered Bill O’Reilly threatening Democrats with legal action Monday morning.

“The Democratic Party in Alaska cheated, and in a big way,” conservative commentator O’Reilly said in the clip, which Trump posted without a caption. “And that’s gonna lead to criminal prosecutions.”

O’Reilly is referring to the Alaska Senate race between incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, in which Republicans have accused Democrats of purposefully attempting to sow confusion on the ballot by running a “Dan J. Sullivan” as an independent alongside their own Dan Sullivan.

Trump preemptively protested the outcome of the race for weeks, calling for a criminal prosecution of Peltola—and for the Justice Department to sue Alaska and block the certification of the vote—if the incumbent Sullivan lost. Trump even went so far as to call for votes for Dan J. Sullivan to go directly to the senator.

While the race has yet to be called, Peltola has pulled away from Sullivan to establish a comfortable lead with 97 percent of the ballots counted.

items.title: Transcript: MAGA Fractures on Hegseth as Trump Iran Humiliation Grows
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 16 episode of The Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

Donald Trump has finally figured out how to look as if he’s won a world-historical triumph over Iran: by doing nothing. Trump has decided not to restart military action, and not to make a deal either. Instead, he’ll wait until the regime collapses.

This comes as officials are suggesting in leaks that Trump is siding with Hegseth in this regard, and against others in the administration who want a deal, including JD Vance. Meanwhile, numerous MAGA figures are rallying behind Hegseth.

The situation is deeply humiliating for Trump. He’s still gotten nothing from Iran, yet he and much of MAGA are basically following Hegseth over a cliff. Is there any way out? We’re making sense out of all of it with former national security official Emily Horne. Thanks for coming on, Emily.

Emily Horne: Great to be with you, Greg.

Sargent: So let’s just quickly situate where we are. Trump now appears to be ruling out new military action against Iran, but his new strategy on Iran is just to wait until economic sanctions topple the Iranian regime. Can you quickly recap where we are, kind of?

Horne: Yeah, unfortunately, I don’t have a lot to add to what you just laid down, because we are in a very strange holding pattern, where there are ships that are moving through the Strait of Hormuz, but they are reliant on U.S. military support in order to do so. So it’s not accurate to say that the strait is open, as President Trump claims.

I don’t think open would include a personal escort by a U.S. aircraft carrier in order to move a shipload of goods or oil through what was previously an open commercial maritime pathway.

That said it’s still better than having open conflict, which is what the Trump administration had been rumor-mongering in the run-up to the midterms, that they were prepared to start massive strikes on both Iranian military and civilian infrastructure.

And so I don’t want to give anyone credit for avoiding yet another illegal war, but it’s worth noting that at least that scenario has not come to pass. The one thing that we know for sure is that the Iranians and the hard-liners and the IRGC really have all the cards right now, and Trump has really nothing to play.

Sargent: In fact, the New York Times’ David Sanger had an absolutely withering piece pointing out how absurd this all is. He noted that it’s not clear that Iran will crack under the sanctions all that soon.

And while oil is coming out of the Strait of Hormuz right now, as you pointed out, we’re spending enormous amounts of money on the U.S. military to enable that to happen. And it’s hard to know how sustainable that is.

And then on top of that, the enriched uranium is still there underground. This is the whole reason Trump went to war. He then claimed he had obliterated the nuclear threat entirely.

Now Trump and his advisers have flipped to saying, it’s no biggie that the uranium is still there, we got this. Trump is winning because he says so. Is that basically the situation we’re in?

Horne: You know, the analogy that I like to use sometimes when you’re talking about Trump and Iran is, do you ever watch South Park? You remember the underpants gnomes? This is Trump’s whole approach to Iran. The underpants gnomes were: Step one, collect underpants. Step two, question mark. Step three, profit. And that’s always been Trump’s approach to Iran.

And to be fair, it’s not just Trump. This has been a lot of hard-liner hawk positions toward Iran, where if you just take unspecified military action toward Iran, then question mark, question mark, question mark, and Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. Trump is just the latest flavor of that particular approach to Iran that we’ve seen for a long time.

Look, the fact remains, at the end of the Obama administration, the United States had a deal with the Iranian regime that would have kept Iran’s nuclear ambitions in check. We were on that path, and Donald Trump walked away from all of that hard work in the first administration that he won.

And everything that we are living through now is the logical outcome of that very foolhardy and shortsighted and, frankly, selfish decision that he made in his first administration to abandon diplomacy.

Sargent: There was even some leaking a while back that Trump was desperately urging his advisers to find some way, any way at all, for him to say that he had gotten more out of Iran than Obama did. And of course nobody could find anything. And so there you have it.

Horne: Yeah, and it turns out you can’t yada-yada your way out of a war. There’s been a lot that Trump has been able to escape consequences on, because he’s a master at manipulating media, and he’s a master at getting people to do his bidding if it makes him feel better about himself.

But when you are talking about deploying aircraft carriers and tens of thousands of troops to adjust our force posture across the Middle East, and trying to negotiate with allies for how they are going to protect their own assets from Iranian missile and drone attacks, you can’t just close your eyes and will it all to go away, or make someone bring you a better talking point that lets you feel bigger and more badass than the president who preceded you. It just doesn’t work like that.

Sargent: No, it doesn’t. And the Post actually shed some light with some reporting on the situation. One official briefed on ongoing discussions leaked word that JD Vance, special envoy Steve Witkoff, and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner privately pushed Trump to make a deal, but Hegseth appeared opposed to one.

Emily, if I’m reading that right, Trump, by not making a deal and sticking to this waiting game of his, is essentially siding with Hegseth, right?

Horne: So I think we have to be really careful when we’re looking at what is essentially a Washington political media that is just a cesspool of people leaking against each other in the Trump administration right now, especially in the aftermath of the midterms.

JD Vance took almost a solid 24 hours after the shellacking of the blue wave on midterms eve to come out, and the first thing that he did was say the Iran war is responsible for Republicans’ losses on election night. And by doing so, he’s trying to differentiate himself from the very administration of which he is literally the vice president.

And so I think what we can know is that, one, people are going to keep leaking on each other, and they’re going to keep doing so with an eye less toward trying to curry favor with Trump, which was their goal for the first two years.

And now that Trump is a lame duck, it’s going to be much more with an eye toward what are their own future paths in Republican politics.

Sargent: Yes. I think we can probably conclude, based on Hegseth’s public posture, which is just nothing but malevolent fury and aggressiveness in basically every guise—we could probably conclude from that that Hegseth really doesn’t want to make a deal. He doesn’t want an easy way out of this thing that looks like any kind of capitulation.

Horne: As long as Trump insists the Iran war is going great, he’s got to stand by the guy he has running it. And to abandon Hegseth now, or to set Hegseth aside, as was rumored immediately after the midterms that Trump was considering doing, would be to admit that he made a mistake with the illegal war against Iran, that his attacks on Iran are not working, that there is no diplomatic or military end in sight in the foreseeable future, and that this is a catastrophe entirely of his own making.

And of course, Trump can’t admit that. He has to insist that the war is going great, because he’s never admitted in his life that he’s made a mistake. And so why would he start now?

Sargent: Well, that’s exactly why MAGA figures are rallying aggressively around Hegseth right now, and they’re in a rage at Hegseth’s critics. Media Matters flagged a bunch of examples. Here’s Fox’s Mark Levin ripping Republican critics of Hegseth.

Mark Levin (voiceover): What a bunch of cowards. We see this with all the isolationists. Pete Hegseth is a patriot.

Here’s influencer Jack Posobiec.

Jack Posobiec (voiceover): And I see a lot of people trying to blame all this on Secretary Hegseth. Don’t think I don’t see it out there. Don’t think I don’t see what’s going on. The blame game’s coming around. No, no, no, no. No, no, no, no. We’re not playing that game. We’re not playing that game. Pete Hegseth is an absolute patriot, and we’re going to leave it at that.

And here’s Hugh Hewitt.

Hugh Hewitt (voiceover): Pete Hegseth has done a great job for two years of executing the president’s orders. The president’s commander in chief. President Trump has done this well. And I think he ought to stick with his national security team, which means Rubio and Hegseth.


Sargent: Emily, these guys are really just following Hegseth over a cliff here, aren’t they?

Horne: I think a lot of them are. And you’re seeing a lot of defense of Hegseth come, unsurprisingly, from his former colleagues at Fox News—a lot of people with whom he has a longstanding personal and professional relationship, but also people who want to protect their access to the Trump administration. They’re defending one of their own, but they’re also defending their turf.

I think, though, it’s important to watch very closely where we’re starting to see some cracks emerging in this coalition. That’s something I’m keeping a really close eye on, especially as we are seeing more and more voices recognize the mandate that Democrats were given in the midterm elections, a lot of which came out of frustration with the Iran war.

And the ensuing rising cost of living—cost of gas, cost of groceries, et cetera—that have come from, yes, tariffs and other foolhardy economic choices, but also this conflict that is now entering its eighth month.

Sargent: Well, let’s just bear down on how humiliating this situation actually is for Trump. One expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told the New York Times this: “Trump began the war thinking he would be a hero. He’s now trying to figure out how to end the war without looking like a loser.”

Another expert, at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said that if Trump leaves the situation as it is, which is what he’s doing, that’s, “a victory for Iran.” Emily, is that basically the situation, the way those two experts described it?

Horne: It’s interesting. I hear that first quote and I think, who the heck was he listening to that was telling him that this would be a quick and easy victory? Because no Iran expert I know thought it would be.

Look, I think there were people in Trump’s inner circle that were telling him Venezuela was a big success: We got in, we got Maduro, we got out, no muss, no fuss. You hear Trump echoing that line of reasoning in his own defense of Iran.

Anyone who knows the tiniest thing about Iran specifically, or the Middle East broadly, about the history of the U.S.-Iran-Israel relationship—you know, take your pick of framing—but anyone who knows anything about that region would have told Trump, had they been asked, this is not going to be the quick and easy win that your inner circle is telling you. And a lot of people, I think, did try to tell him that in various ways.

Iran has all of the leverage right now. They control access to the Strait of Hormuz. They control the pace and the tempo of proxy strikes across the region. This is terrible to say, but that they do not care about the suffering of their own people is a strategic asset for them in this moment.
