Because they are perfectly willing to let Iranian civilians bear the brunt of the humanitarian catastrophe that is coming to them via not just strikes, but the effects of sanctions and other forms of economic punishment that don’t impact the elites of the regime, but very much harm the life of the average, everyday Iranian.

So yeah, they have all of the leverage right now. And, you know, we don’t know what their demands have been exactly in the diplomatic negotiations that have happened to date, but I would be willing to venture they’re probably pretty maximalist.

They probably run along some line of, let us maintain control of the Strait of Hormuz, or at the very least impose tolls, which they have never done before. And now it’s hard to imagine a world in which they would not derive tremendous economic benefit from controlling access to the strait.

That bell cannot be unrung, and that’s entirely thanks to Donald Trump. But more broadly, that they would tell Trump pound sand on anything that we want to do vis-à-vis our nuclear program, and we’re just going to keep doing what we’re doing, and you’re just going to have to deal with it.

Sargent: Just to refer back to what one of those experts said, the fact that Trump is looking for a way to appear not to be a loser just is the real story in a nutshell, and everybody knows it.

And the entire national security apparatus around Trump, and the entire GOP, they’re all required to pretend this isn’t what’s happening. They must maintain the illusion that Trump is currently winning a glorious triumph. It’s almost like the North Korean dictator has no clothes, right?

Horne: Well, and it’s really interesting, because we are seeing a split that is emerging around Iran. We’ve talked earlier about the Fox News crowd, who need to protect their access to and relationship with Trump.

But there’s a different audience, a podcast and independent content creator and radio audience—they have their own audiences. They are young. They are more anti-war. They were people who voted for Trump in 2024 because of his promise of no new foreign wars and lower costs. They are not dyed-in-the-wool MAGA. They do not maintain the same loyalties. And a lot of them turned out for Democrats in the midterms this year.

And so you’re starting to see the influencers and content creators and hosts who reach primarily those audiences start to sing a very different tune than the Fox News crowd. Because this is not an ideological split for them. This is a business model split.

Sargent: Well, what’s the way out? Is it just essentially waiting for Democrats to take over and hoping, really, really hoping, that they make good on their threat so far to defund the Iran war? Is that the only way this gets resolved?

Horne: Look, Democrats were elected last week to do two things: affordability and accountability. And Iran sits right in the middle of those two priorities. So Democrats defunding Trump’s illegal war in Iran are going to be able to help bring down gas prices, the prices of goods and services.

But they’re also going to get America out of a war that it has no business being in. They’re going to cut back on the war profiteers who have figured out, whether through the prediction markets or through their investments in oil futures, how to personally profit from this war, while the average person can’t afford a pack of hamburger at the grocery store the way they used to.

I think people are really tired of the sense that a small group of elites are figuring out how to profit from the very kind of wars that Trump said he was not going to get us into anymore. And people are impatient for change. And defunding the Iran war is a great place to start delivering on the request for those changes.

Sargent: OK. When Democrats take over in January, do you think Pete Hegseth will still be there? Yes or no?

Horne: Yeah, probably. Look, I think a lot of things about Massie’s attempt to impeach Hegseth, and we could have a whole separate conversation on that. But the top line is that it actually wound up really securing Hegseth’s job, at least for the next couple of months.

Because here’s what: This is an administration where being under attack is their comfort zone, and something like an impeachment attempt actually becomes a credential. In Trump world, getting impeached proves that you’re on the right side. And before the midterms, Trump was rumored to be asking his associates, I don’t know about this Hegseth guy, what do you think about him? Which is usually a precursor to someone getting fired in a very public and embarrassing way.

Instead, Thomas Massie impeached Pete Hegseth, or tried to, and he gave him a lifeline and a storyline—a storyline where he was able to hold a news conference at the Pentagon and say, I’m under attack. There he was able to stand behind the troops and use our military as a shield.

And he also probably overreached by introducing eight articles of impeachment, some of which Republicans may have agreed with, but some of which they would have said, I don’t know about that. And so if and when there is a Democratic impeachment movement against Pete Hegseth, I would expect that it would be more limited in scope, and it would be far more competently executed.

Sargent: So I guess that really means we’re going to have to absolutely hold Democrats to their pledge to defund this thing. Otherwise, we’re really screwed. But I think they probably will do it. Emily Horne, awesome to have you on.

Folks, if you want more of Emily, you can check out her Substack, which is called Spin Class. Emily, thanks so much for coming on.

Horne: Thanks, Greg. Great to be with you.

items.title: How Zohran Mamdani Uses Sports to Spread the Gospel of Progressivism
items.content_text:
On a brisk late-October afternoon on Coney Island, the home field of the minor league, Mets-affiliated Brooklyn Cyclones was taken over by a more international pastime. Miniature soccer nets polka-dotted the baseball diamond as amateurs sent soccer balls streaking across the mosaic horizon of Luna Park’s usual attractions: the Wonder Wheel, the Cyclone, the Thunderbolt. They had come here to battle one another in the second Cost of Living Classic, a free-to-enter five-a-side soccer tournament hosted by the city of New York and its mayor—and die-hard fan of the English Premier League’s Arsenal FC—Zohran Mamdani.

Players in the tournament were split into beginner and advanced divisions, then randomly assigned to teams with names like “Affordability Arsenal,” “Corruption Attackers,” and “200,000 Potgoals Filled”—a reference to the thousands of potholes the mayor has filled in his term thus far, which are among his signature accomplishments.

Over the course of the afternoon, behind classic global soccer jams like “Baianá” and “Waka Waka,” the tournament was gradually whittled down to just two teams per division, with “Place the PK” duking it out with “Affordability Arsenal” in the beginners’ finale. “The mayor’s watching,” the emcee warned both teams over the loudspeaker as they set up for overtime, before “Place the PK” ultimately prevailed in penalty kicks.

The tournament was the latest in a long string of efforts from the New York City mayor to fold sports culture into his political platform. It’s also the result of a larger belief that politics is most effective when it meets people where they already are. “At a personal level, sports is just a huge part of my life. It’s how I understood myself and the world,” Mamdani told me as we stood in Maimonides Park’s spartan press box, watching the pickup tournament below. “On a political level, it’s also a reflection of the fact that that’s the case for so many New Yorkers. Sports is what they live for, they dream of, they breathe, and we can’t think of it as separate from our politics because it is political whether or not someone can afford to go and watch their team.”

A recreational league soccer player, Mamdani keeps in touch with friends by playing pickup basketball now that he’s mayor. And sports are not just a key part of his administration; they are essential to understanding the mayor’s approach to politics itself. He has hosted watch parties, built new tennis courts and soccer fields, and used every opportunity to connect sports with his progressive values. It helped, of course, that New York had a summer for the ages this year, as the Knicks won their first NBA Championship since 1973 and the city co-hosted eight World Cup games, including the final, at MetLife stadium in nearby Rutherford, New Jersey.

For decades, sports have been the cultural domain of the right, and in recent years they have emerged as a staple of MAGA conservatism. President Donald Trump routinely campaigns with athletes like Brett Favre and Danica Patrick and attends Ultimate Fighting Championship events—one of which took place on the White House lawn in July, as part of the administration’s celebration of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence—and football games, which he uses as an extension of his own pugilistic politics. In New York, Mamdani and his allies are building a progressive counterbalance that privileges egalitarian ideals, public infrastructure, and accessibility. In less than a year, there are already signs that it’s working.


The right has typically used sports as a kind of stage on which to display its values. “Republicans root their politics much more around these mythic images,” said historian Rick Perlstein, who has written several books about the conservative movement, including Nixonland and Reaganland. “These simulated gladiatorial combats,” Perlstein said, “suit a certain kind of right-wing vision of the world, binary thinking, good versus evil, playing by the rules.” For half a century, stretching from die-hard football fan Richard Nixon to the UFC-obsessed Trump, conservatives have had a decided edge, particularly by embracing patriotism, rugged individualism, and violence.

Trump has not only continued that tradition but, as Perlstein describes it, launched it into the “stratosphere.” He regularly appears alongside current and former players and coaches and has a particular affinity for football players, boxers, and other practitioners of combat sports. He has a long-standing alliance with the UFC’s CEO, Dana White. White played a key role in Trump’s 2024 victory, first by engineering a series of appearances at UFC fights that helped rehabilitate his image after January 6, and then by brokering appearances on a series of podcasts with huge followings among young men, a cohort that helped propel him to victory.

At one of Trump’s first public appearances as president-elect in 2024, a UFC fight night at Madison Square Garden, attendees told me his yearslong relationship with the UFC had helped convince them of his relatability, his everyman nature. These appearances helped pull off a political magic trick of sorts and project an aura of masculinity and strength despite his being an overweight, older politician who had spent his long life ensconced in luxury. They also served as a key tool of a larger political project rooted in violence and domination.

“ Being able to appear just a handful of months after that insurrection, when still most Republicans wouldn’t speak to him … and to be cheered the way he was, was significant,” said Karim Zidan, author of The Ultimate Strongmen: MMA and the Rise of the New Authoritarian Right. Those appearances, Zidan argued, “ were pivotal to Donald Trump’s reelection.”


Historically, Democrats haven’t been able to use sports to nearly the same effect. During his 2008 and 2012 campaigns, Barack Obama touted endorsements from LeBron James, Magic Johnson, and Muhammad Ali, and used his pickup basketball prowess to tout an everyman image. But few in the party have embraced sports as a vehicle for identity politics and metaphor as Republicans have. Mamdani isn’t just trying to use sports differently; he’s trying to get his fellow Democrats and progressives to view sports differently. “The very understanding of what leisure and rest [are] is the result of political fights that have been won and sustained,” Mamdani told me.

If Mamdani’s evocation of leisure and rest hearkens back to some of the earliest fights of the progressive movement, it also helps explain what events like the Cost of Living Classic are really about. The point isn’t just to underscore his argument that New Yorkers’ lives should be more affordable; it’s to give people something meaningful to do on their day off.

“[Politics] shouldn’t just be nuts and bolts. It should also be fun and joyous,” Mamdani’s press secretary, Joe Calvello, told me. “ As someone who believes in excellence in government, that means making sure working-class New Yorkers can actually enjoy their city.” Calvello, a former Division I lacrosse player, is one of several figures in the administration who resemble their boss, which is to say he’s a jock and a sports fan. Calvello described Trump’s embrace of the UFC, in particular, as an “extremely savvy play.”

Mamdani has embraced sports from the moment he took office earlier this year. Understanding the significance of hosting the World Cup in ways most previous mayors likely would not have, Mamdani announced watch parties and family-friendly fan zones in all five boroughs, opened temporary playing fields, and called out FIFA for “price gouging.”

At the same time, he showcased a pragmatic streak that has defined the first year of his term as mayor. Although he criticized FIFA publicly, he did so while working behind the scenes to secure 1,000 affordable tickets he then raffled off to New Yorkers. At New York’s first World Cup game, he split his time between New York Governor Kathy Hochul’s skybox and the people who won discounted tickets. When the mayor attended game 3 of the NBA Finals, he did so on his own dime, coughing up $1,000 for a standing room ticket.

During the U.S. Open later in the summer, he pulled off the same maneuver and got over a thousand discounted tickets from the United States Tennis Association. Hundreds of thousands of people entered raffles for these tranches of discounted tickets, which double as evidence that Mamdani is following through on his core campaign promise: to make one of the most expensive cities in the world more affordable.

The USTA also pledged hundreds of thousands to refurbish public tennis courts across the city. These projects are just as important as the tranches of discounted tickets. Indeed, building and maintaining sporting infrastructure across the city has been a key part of Mamdani’s mayoralty. The newly minted “Renew Crew” has repaired dozens of basketball, handball, and tennis courts, outfitted lights for nighttime play, and extended a pilot program that keeps soccer fields open until the early hours of the morning.

It is astronomically cheaper and faster to renovate a tennis court or switch out the net on a basketball hoop than it is to build public housing or renovate a subway station. These types of sporting renovations sit squarely within the purview of the mayor’s powers, meaning that he can enact them quickly and efficiently without requiring coordination with other governmental or regulatory bodies.

The idea that sports provide an opportunity to reach people who aren’t reached by ordinary political messaging is at the center of much of Mamdani’s sports policy. Just as important is the opportunity for public programs and infrastructure to bring together people who might not ordinarily interact—and to allow more to watch sporting and cultural events that can be expensive to stream, let alone attend.

“Think about the story of travel soccer across this country. Of a lot of club sports for kids,” Mamdani told me, referring to the prohibitively high—and rising—cost of many private youth sports. “There’s so much of a class dynamic to it that is often overlooked,” he continued. “We should want people to be playing sports. It is good for their body. It is good for their mind. It is good for our society, and yet we’re making it something that people can be priced out of.”

For Mamdani, these efforts achieve several goals simultaneously: They reach voters who might not be plugged into politics, push the mayor’s affordability-based agenda, and make the government present in ways it often isn’t. Indeed, much of his politics can be understood as a kind of war against abstraction. Just as the mayor makes a big deal of filling potholes, events like the Cost of Living Classic exist as evidence that New York City’s government is visibly, actively present in its communities and cultural life.

Across the ideological spectrum, politicians typically use sports mainly for electoral ends: Fandom and athletic pursuits can emphasize relatability or highlight youth and virility, while celebrity endorsements aim to harness one kind of fandom in service of another. Mamdani and his administration are up to something altogether different: They are using sports as a tool to highlight broader initiatives around affordability, access, and public infrastructure. Events like the Cost of Living Classic aren’t just meant to interact with constituents who might otherwise tune out politics; they’re intended to serve as a form of civic engagement itself. Rather than trying to convince people to trust him because he loves sports, too, Mamdani is making it easier for them to share with one another the sports they love.

Maya Handa—who was tasked with managing the logistical implementation of the World Cup, which brought more than 1.2 million people to the New York-New Jersey area—agrees that progressives have often steered clear of involving themselves in sports. There’s some perception that sports bring out an ugliness, a factionalism, or an aggression, Handa said. “But actually, sports also bring out ... teamwork and joy … and a kind of patriotism that can be good.”

Addressing the crowd shortly after the conclusion of the Cost of Living Classic, Mamdani made a similar pitch. “ It’s a political question whether or not New Yorkers can afford to have fun. It’s a political question whether or not New Yorkers can get out there and be a part of the people’s game,” he said. “And we want this to be a city where soccer isn’t just something that you can watch on TV or watch highlight reels of, but it’s also something that you can actually be a part of.” For what it’s worth, the mayor had provided confetti and champagne—the nonalcoholic kind—for the winners.

items.title: The Best Case Against Schumer and Jeffries Is Geography, Not Ideology
items.content_text:
The Democratic Party just did something pretty remarkable. It expanded its congressional presence into regions of the country and states where it had been dead as a doornail for a decade or longer. Dems won big races in Ohio. They did the same in Iowa. They won in Kansas and Montana and South Carolina and Kentucky and Texas and Mississippi. They have a national footprint of a sort they haven’t had since the early 1990s, when, in the 102nd Congress, they controlled 56 seats in the Senate and 267 in the House.

You might think they’d want leadership teams that reflect this geographic power and diversity. After all, one of the right’s favorite attack lines against Democrats is that they’re a party of big-city coastal elites with no foothold in, or feeling for, the American heartland. In this light, then, I pose a question to you: Is it a problem that the two men who are likely to lead the party in the next Congress live about one mile away from each other, in a city the rest of the country doesn’t particularly like?

Chuck Schumer lives along Brooklyn’s glorious Prospect Park. Hakeem Jeffries lives just a few blocks to the north. Yes, it’s a mere coincidence. And yes, I love Brooklyn. I lived in (I think) five different apartments in the County of Kings over the 20 years I lived in New York.

But my feelings about the place, or anyone else’s, aren’t the issue here. The issue is how the Democratic Party presents itself to the nation. And one way not to be caricatured as a party of New York City and San Francisco is … to have leaders who aren’t from New York City and San Francisco.

Before I mount that horse, let’s consider Jeffries and Schumer and their other merits and demerits. This Wednesday, House Democrats are expected to vote to make Jeffries their leader (the official vote to make him the next speaker of the House will take place next January 3). There’s no way Democrats are going to deny the speakership to the first Black man in history in line to hold that position. No serious challenge to Jeffries has emerged, and none is likely to; he and his team have been aggressive in preemptively fighting off such challenges and making support for him appear to be as unanimous as possible.

At the same time, there’s considerable grumpiness on Bluesky (natch) and in certain progressive circles about this presumed coronation. It reflects three concerns: one, that he wasn’t a more effective opposition leader in the first year of Donald Trump’s second term (things improved some in year two); two, his perceived and in some cases real coziness to corporate donors and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee; three, a sense, stemming from the first two points, that he’s not the man to lead the charge on either reining in Trumpian corruption or passing aggressively populist legislation that will tell the multibillionaires and monopolists that the party’s over.

I think Jeffries has taken some fair shots and some unfair ones over the years, but you can count me among those who share concern number three. On investigating Trump, it was not reassuring that the day after the big win, he defaulted to saying “the American people don’t want us to get even” and dismissing legitimate and necessary investigations into acts of obvious illegality and unconstitutionality as “retribution.” He just doesn’t sound like someone who has a zest for the fight.

On economic matters, this son of two union members has never been a populist. People are watching very closely to see how big he’s willing to go. At the party’s conference last week in Denver, he did say that after reversing the Trump Medicaid cuts and restoring the Obamacare subsidies, the House would move to lower the Medicare eligibility age and extend coverage to hearing, vision, and dental coverage.

Some will complain that it’s not Medicare for All, but M4A involves substantial tax increases that of necessity are going to be the topic of a lengthy debate. The above change, if the House passes it, would constitute a significant step in that direction.

Of course, to mean anything, it has to pass the Senate too—which brings us to Schumer.

If the Democratic base is grudgingly willing to give Jeffries his shot, the verdict on Schumer is far less mixed. He’s five points underwater among Democrats in a recent CNN poll. Said the network’s Harry Enten: “He’s the least popular Democratic leader in the United States Senate since at least 1985.”

I’ve known and watched Schumer for a long time. He has clear strengths and clear weaknesses. He’s a great nose-counter, horse-trader, and cat-herder; he knows how to get stuff passed. He did that very well during Biden’s presidency. In other words, he is, literally, a skilled majority leader.

But when the party’s in the minority, that’s when his weak points come to the fore. He’s not a street fighter or a hellraiser. He’s an establishment guy. It just isn’t in his DNA to be a swashbuckling opposition leader. Leading a legislative majority and leading a legislative minority are two completely different jobs, so much so that I’ve come around to the belief that Democrats should officially make them two different jobs: Elevate someone with the majority-leader skill set when they’re in the majority, then switch to someone with the minority-leader skill set when they’re in the minority.

The next Congress presents a bit of puzzle, because, while the Democrats will be in the majority in the Senate, the president will still be a Republican (and not just any Republican). The Democrats will want to pass bills, of course, but opposing Trump will still be a big part of the job; arguably still the main part of the job.

Enter Chris Van Hollen, who’s challenging Schumer for the leadership. It’s not clear how much of a hellraiser he is, but his trip to El Salvador to try to see Kilmar Ábrego García and his vocal opposition to Israel’s cruelly excessive post–October 7 violence in Gaza have won him the progressives’ stamp of approval. The more left-leaning groups are pushing his candidacy hard. The secret ballot vote is scheduled for Tuesday, December 1.

I’d still rate Van Hollen as a long shot. Schumer has been the Democrats’ leader for a decade now. That’s a lot of favors he’s done for a lot of senators. And senators just aren’t boat-rockers. The stodginess of the place is practically in the water. Schumer seems to have the votes right now, which is why he and his people are pushing to have the vote before December 1.

It’s getting acrimonious. On ABC’s This Week Sunday, Van Hollen took aim at the argument that Schumer’s supporters have advanced since the election and that the conventional wisdom seems to have bought completely: that Schumer led the Democrats to this historic victory. As ABC’s Martha Raddatz put it to Van Hollen, quoting one Schumer-backing senator: “Why would you fire the manager who just won the World Series?”

Van Hollen had an answer, and it was a good one: “Let’s be real. This was not a Washington-orchestrated election around the country. This was the American people rising up against a lawless president and demanding change. We won not just Senate seats and House seats. We won governor’s races. We won legislative races.”

He’s totally right. Schumer deserves credit for recruiting winning candidates in some cases. But in other cases, he opposed winners. He opposed Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota in their primaries. In Maine, he wanted Janet Mills, who flamed out quickly and excited no one. National Democrats only moved to help Scott Colom in Mississippi very late in the game, and they did nothing for Angie Nixon in Florida and Jamie Davis in Louisiana, both of whom could have won with some help.

So Schumer’s record in these midterms was actually mixed. The team won the World Series, but the manager made some questionable decisions about the pitching rotation.

Even if Van Hollen doesn’t win, we can hope that his challenge to Schumer can get the latter to agree to some things that he could just ignore if he didn’t face a challenge. The most important among these is the filibuster.

The House will pass all these nice things, like restoring Obamacare subsidies. But then, if the filibuster isn’t changed or eliminated, they’ll go to the Senate and die. Schumer and other filibuster defenders will blow a lot of smoke at us about how they think they can work with a chastened Republican Party and get those four votes to end cloture and move to a final vote, which requires 60 votes.

But it’ll be nonsense. In most cases, no Republican will want to be that sixtieth vote. Doing so would guarantee them a well-funded and possibly career-ending primary. So none of these lovely things will pass the Senate. And to most voters it’ll just look like the same old dysfunction.

A conversation about the filibuster has at least started. Van Hollen said in Denver that he personally opposes the filibuster, and he committed at least to debating it if elected leader: “This is an issue that I think we need to talk to the caucus about.” And Schumer last week didn’t rule out eliminating the filibuster. This is a huge development, and it wouldn’t be happening if Schumer were waltzing to recoronation.

As of today, it seems that these two neighbors who live a 15-minute walk away from each other will probably lead their caucuses. If Schumer wins, it will presumably be his last term. For Jeffries, it could be the start of a long tenure. But whatever the future holds for these two, the Democrats have to take full advantage of the astonishing geographic mandate the voters just gave them.

At the very least, they need to elevate their candidates who won in red states and let America see that there are Democrats from places like Kentucky and South Carolina and that, on economics at least, they’re pretty populist. The midterms have handed them the opportunity to decimate the image of them as representing only coastal big cities. They need to seize it.

items.title: The Extraordinary Vision of Lee Krasner
items.content_text:
In 1939, in a Greenwich Village studio on East Ninth Street, a determined young artist had a friend paint these lines from Arthur Rimbaud’s A Season in Hell across her wall:

To whom shall I hire myself out? What beast must I adore? What holy image is attacked? What hearts shall I break? What lie must I maintain? — In what blood tread?

Rimbaud’s poem is, in the words of Patti Smith, “the formula for the alchemical transformation of the soul.” The artist was Lee Krasner, and this was indeed her project: She believed that making art was the most honest and revolutionary of acts. If it took exhausting and breaking yourself, so be it.

Krasner is one-half of the two-artist show on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art through January, “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” a gloriously surprising and immensely moving exhibition that sets out to explore the creative partnership between Krasner and her husband, an artist you may have heard of named Jackson Pollock.

As critic Johanna Fateman admits in her catalog essay, the show’s setup is a perilous endeavor. It is perilous because it seems impossible—who can hold their own against Pollock’s shine?—and because it is overdetermined. Eclipsed by Pollock’s celebrity, Krasner has been alternately forgotten, written off as derivative of her husband, or—come the women’s liberation movement—seen as a tragic feminist figure blunted from making her best work by a drunken man-child. She refused all caricatures. In a questionnaire, Krasner was once asked to list the greatest sacrifice she ever made for her art. “I sacrificed nothing,” she wrote.

Under the sensitive curation of David Breslin and Brinda Kumar, “Krasner and Pollock” shows that she was right. More: It shows that she did indeed transform her soul—and all of modern art.


Lee Krasner was born Lena Krassner to an Orthodox Jewish family in Brownsville, Brooklyn, in 1908. Her family had come from the shtetl in Russia’s Pale of Settlement; her eldest siblings were born there. Her father told her fairy tales—“marvelous tales!”—which delighted her, with their dark forests, snow, and sleighs; her brother read her Maurice Maeterlinck, the Belgian symbolist, in translation. With this schooling in symbology, it’s no surprise that young Lena soon went to the library looking for the kinds of images she saw in her mind. Realizing that the Jewish morning prayer had separate endings for men and for women, she refused, anymore, to say it. As soon as she could, she left suburban Brooklyn for a series of art schools in Manhattan, moved to Greenwich Village, and rechristened herself “Lee.”

Throughout the 1920s and 1930s, Krasner moved through a series of art schools, worked for the WPA, organized with the new Depression-era Artists Union, became a Trotskyist as opposed to a Stalinist, broke up with a lover, and went looking for something more. In 1937, she began working with the legendary European teacher Hans Hofmann, whose strict and stark atelier helped bring so much of European modernism to hungry artists in the States. He was known for his rigor and his force—it was not uncommon for him to rip up and ­rearrange students’ work to illustrate a point. Hofmann’s comment on seeing Krasner’s work was, “This is so good, you would not know it was done by a woman.” Her skill is evident in the first gallery, showing her early work alongside Pollock’s: You can see how her rigorous classical training worked her through every style and into the cubism and surrealism coming out of Paris. She tried on everything, had a taste for the French, committed herself to abstract painting around 1937. Soon, she was considered to have the best eye for modern art in New York.


Jackson Pollock was born into a troubled family, with an ambitious and frustrated mother, and an alcoholic, socialist, withdrawn father, who—in an attempt to toughen sons he believed to be overmothered—forced all his boys to help as he castrated the family’s farm animals. Jackson, the sensitive and imaginative baby of the family, born in 1912, grew up into a rebellious, alcoholic teenager, alternately spoiled, bullied, and protected by his band of brothers.

He was a man for whom conventional masculinity was a puzzle. A sensitive child, he preferred to be the mama when he played house and kept his teddy bear on his bed long past when he thought he should. Yet growing up in the West, first in Wyoming, then Arizona and California, he was presented with a cowboy vision of manhood, one to which he fitfully tried to conform. In 1931, he went hitchhiking and train-hopping, riding the rails between Kansas and California with hoboes, just as self-consciously interested in American mythmaking as was his later spiritual brother Jack Kerouac. He returned to his family in Los Angeles a terrified physical wreck, having definitely been jailed and, according to his biographers Steven Naifeh and Gregory White Smith, likely been raped by predatory older men. Throughout his life, his friends talked of a Dr. Jekyll/Mr. Hyde split in his personality: the shy, polite, fame-averse, sensitive man, and the raging wild drunk, hurling abuse and thick with bravado and misogynist charisma.

One of the extraordinary things about Pollock was his determination to express what tore at him. He was not, as his brothers Charles and Sande were, a natural artistic talent. As his biographers write, his classes with the regionalist painter Thomas Hart Benton at New York’s Art Students League in the early ’30s “revealed a lack of control over a pencil that at times verged on a physical disability.” As a classmate remembers, “Jack fought paint and brushes all the way.” The early sketches of his in the Met show reveal this—energy and ardent imagination, but a hand unable to represent what he so obviously saw, figures with the hard-to-draw faces and hands left unfinished.

Instead of working harder to learn his craft, Pollock threw tantrums in class, became borderline inarticulate, and expressed himself in weeklong suicidal binges in the Bowery. Drinking made him exceptionally cruel: He once threatened to chop a woman’s head off with an ax he held just above her, finally sinking it into his brother’s best painting on the wall behind.

Yet there was something about his lack of technique that became a kind of superpower: His work was all energy, all expression, uncontained. To fight your tools, after all, means you’re imparting the drama of force to the canvas. The curators have hung both Krasner’s and Pollock’s contributions to John Graham’s 1942 show “American and French Paintings” across from each other in a small room: In Krasner’s Blue Square (1940–1942), thick with impasto, you see a painting that is accomplished but dead; its artist still needs to slough off the traditions she has studied. Pollock’s Birth (1941), on the other hand, is roiling and arresting—full of eyes and totems, beaks and color. This was the painting that made Krasner fall in love with him.


The story Krasner and Pollock told is that, in late 1941, Krasner, hearing there was a painter she didn’t know hanging in Graham’s show with her, knocked on the door of his studio and demanded to see his work. The paintings of this shy, inarticulate man hit her as hard as had Picasso’s Guernica: “I was confronted with something ahead of me. I felt elation. My God, there it is.”

In fact, as Krasner later admitted, Pollock had approached her five years prior at one of the Artists Union dances, where he was notorious for causing drunken scenes and harassing women. He cut in on Krasner’s dancing partner, and drawing her close, asked, “Do you like to fuck?” When she felt him rubbing his erection against her leg like a dog, she slapped him across the face.

But despite this, on second meeting, she fell in love with his art, and with him, deeply. They became each other’s primary artistic influences. By 1943, they were inseparable; in 1945, they were married. They moved from the city to the more peaceful hamlet of Springs, in East Hampton, Long Island, where they bought a wood-shingled old house on Fireplace Road. Pollock insisted on supporting both of them with sales of his own work, which were largely nonexistent. They had so little money that they got around on bicycles, and Pollock would dig with his toes on the beach to find clams for dinner. But they had a boat and a goat, a pet dog and a pet crow, and it was their most peaceful time together; they planted mimosa trees, gardened, canned, cooked (Krasner), baked pies (Pollock), and watched the light fade in the evenings.

In other ways, it was not idyllic, as Krasner had, artistically speaking, lost her way. When they had met, she was the self-assured, talented artist, he the upstart. But as Krasner’s contemporary Elaine de Kooning remarked, “it was almost as though Jackson took over something that Lee had had.” Krasner admitted as much: “When we began going together, my own work became irrelevant. He was the important thing. I couldn’t do enough for him.” Among the things she couldn’t do enough of: acting as his publicist and gallery agent; negotiating his first contract with Peggy Guggenheim’s influential gallery; mailing announcements and making publicity calls for his shows, which she would supervise, coordinate, and sometimes staff; caring for him in his habitual drunken binges and his periodic breakdowns; making excuses for both to colleagues; watching him flirt provocatively with other women; holding him during his tantrums, like a toddler, until he quieted. The one thing she wouldn’t do, which he could never forgive, was have a child. One, she told him—meaning him—was all she could handle.

Seeing Krasner’s work from this period is brutal, and it is one of the strengths of this show that the Met doesn’t shy away from that fact. For three years, she created and destroyed painting after painting, turning the canvas into a gray slab of layered paint and then scraping it off—while he thrived. Through two dark corner galleries, we see the contrast: Pollock pushes cubist figures and surrealist symbols to the edge in paintings like The Moon Woman (1942) and Guardians of the Secret (1943), besotted with color, as if Manhattan’s grids had broken open to trees, flowers, sea, sky. Eventually, he jumps off the cliff: Finally able to make large-scale work in the old barn on their property, in 1947 he creates his first drip-technique paintings. They appear, fantastically, to move of their own accord. The curators have placed the kinetic drip work Lucifer (1947) and the luminous Number 13A, 1948: Arabesque on adjacent corners, and standing between the two of them, the air nearly buzzes.

Krasner literally clawed her way out of her gray slab period with Image Surfacing (1945), a shaky blue-and-red surrealist-tinged abstraction scored with deep scratch marks. From here, she moved into a phase known as her “Little Images” period, works from which are dutifully hung by the Met but are as boring as they sound—paintings cramped and confined, repetitive and patterned, as if she’s trying to work out a runic code. She tried her hand at Pollock’s drip technique in this period, but the show doesn’t even have to point out that these feel like caged versions of his: Seeing them side by side here is enough. The one bright spot is Krasner’s 1947 Mosaic Table, a project she began because it was too cold to paint upstairs in the small spare bedroom—a wagon wheel laid flat and inlaid with cement and a bright dynamic swirl of broken glass, coins, keys, and tiles, the only point of generative propulsion in all her work from these years.


The centerpiece of the show is a large, bright room with freestanding walls, so you can get as close to as many of the paintings as you like. We come, first, to those holding Pollock’s mature mural-size masterpieces, the famous works from 1950 to 1952. It doesn’t matter how many times you’ve seen a reproduction: In person, these massive works change you. My favorite is One: Number 31, 1950, a synaptic tangle of dun and gray, black and white, sage and bright green. I sat in front of it until, like those old Magic Eye optical illusions, it took on three dimensions, began to pulse, sprout like so many fungi, crackle like seared skin, swirl like seaweed in the tide, bright as the animating impulse of all life. The feeling was akin to floating and sinking both. This is it, I thought, unconsciously echoing Krasner. Pollock touched God. The world agreed: In 1949, Life magazine asked, “Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?”

The Pollock legend will tell you the costs of this greatness fell, like a Greek tragedy, onto him—his alcoholism, his demons. But in reality, the costs fell on Krasner. Isolated in Springs, she turned inward. The painter Grace Hartigan remembers visiting the couple: “I thought of them equally as artists but she was working against a barrier of ego…. She deliberately submerged her personality to his genius.” Krasner first painted in a cramped corner of the kitchen, moving upstairs to the spare bedroom when Pollock left it once the barn was fixed up. She rose before he did in order to paint and, as one of her friends remembered, was so habituated to his alcohol abuse, lack of control, and his tempers that “the slightest change in her husband’s mood could change her work.” When the success of her mosaic table brought her back to painting, Pollock’s enthusiastic encouragement was quickly replaced by a narcissist’s envy, and he began referring to her Little Images series as “Lee’s little painting.” At a 1948 dinner hosted by a prominent gallery owner celebrating a successful showing of Krasner’s work, Pollock drank to excess, insulted his hostess, destroyed the apartment’s costly antiques. The gallery never booked Krasner again.

1950 was the pinnacle of Pollock’s success, a famous “coming out” year for what was now called the New York School, or simply, abstract expressionism. It was also the year when, in the words of biographer Mary Gabriel, “As Pollock’s notoriety grew, Lee’s very existence had become eclipsed.” On Krasner’s side, this may have been a choice made in service to great art, but it was abusive and unabashedly manipulative on Pollock’s. In 1954, writer Patsy Southgate came to visit her new neighbors and found Krasner in “a state of collapse ... trapped in the house.” She couldn’t drive, though he could and did, in a flashy car he had bought with his earnings, despite their money worries. According to Southgate, “Jackson didn’t want her to [drive], but he had mobility. He would go off, he had his large studio, this person making delicious food, and pretty much what he wanted.” Southgate, appalled, taught Krasner how to drive.

Invigorated by this injection of new life outside of her home, Krasner, finally, stopped apologizing for her husband and began making work again—extraordinary work. The second half of the central gallery is devoted to eight large paintings, all from 1955, arranged in a kind of grove with four paintings encircling the viewer. They are vital, singing works, full of strong, dark verticals and moments of bright color. I stood in the middle and gave them the same attention I had paid to Pollock’s One: Number 31, 1950. Their effect is just as forceful but wholly different: I felt not erased into ether but somehow more powerfully myself, a necessary part of a larger whole. Staring at Milkweed (1955), with its careful layering, precision, and restrained exuberant touches of orange, I understood: The power of Pollock’s best work is that he accesses something immense but is unable to control it—it dissipates outward in those long strings of drip. His are paintings whose drama comes from seeing a weak vessel break apart. These works of Krasner’s, done when she was so ill with ulcerative colitis from the stress of tending him that she could barely walk up stairs, are paintings of a woman who has touched that same thing but been strong enough to channel it.


From 1953 onward, the tables had turned; Krasner was now, finally, doing significant work, having moved out from under her male influences—Matisse and Mondrian, Hofmann and Pollock. Pollock was stuck, drinking heavily, unable to work, terrified of fame, and, by early 1956, carrying on an open affair with a twentysomething (he was 44). He died that August as the worst version of himself—unable to paint and wildly drunk, Pollock took his mistress and her friend for a night ride, while they begged him, crying, to slow down. Only the mistress survived the crash. Reportedly, he laughed as the women screamed.

This show is centered around the idea of a creative partnership, thoughtfully figured by curators Breslin and Kumar in their introductory essay to the catalog as a “collage,” each piece its own, a relation of tension as well as correspondence—and a form that Krasner often worked with. In this view, asking who influenced whom, who was the greater artist, is superfluous.

For all that it’s easy to denigrate Pollock—which he deserves a hundredfold—it’s also true that, in brief and brilliant moments, he and Krasner together were greater than the sum of their parts. “Is this a painting?” Pollock would ask her, while she would incorporate scraps from his discarded works into her collages. They made each other possible, and an entanglement at once romantic, artistic, emotional, and intellectual between two brilliant creative minds is something that it takes a lifetime to parse, if ever. The stakes, and the costs, were high; the problem was, the costs were paid only by her.

Many things are true at once: It is true he nearly killed her; it is true she made him a celebrity (after he died, she quadrupled prices for his work). It is true her suffering allowed for his greatest work; it is true that he helped her move into important new artistic terrain. It is true that, when news of his death reached her in Paris, Krasner collapsed in grief and had to be restrained from the balcony; and it is also true that, after he died, she moved into his old studio in the barn and created huge and joyous, riotously colorful work.

Even Krasner’s grief paintings, the “Night Journeys,” have soft curves, offset by a sharp gesture—a woman mourning, but who has not lost the world.

The show closes largely with Krasner’s works from 1956 to 1977, and the later galleries are designed so that the viewer is pushed through a kind of maze with a revelation around each turn. Now that she no longer had to be the stable one, Krasner let go, exploring both her grief and the bright world that had rushed back to her—most notably, in The Seasons (1957), with its pomegranate shapes, its verdant abundance. Even her grief paintings, the “Night Journeys” made during a bout of insomnia, have soft curves, offset by a sharp gesture—a woman mourning, but who has not lost the world.

And that is what her late work is—an enchantment with the world, organic motifs and shapes, growing and taking root altogether. Late blooming, perhaps, this is an artist who has fought her way to her own garden and then painted the rich abundance she saw there. Rising Green (1972) is a perfect painting, and sees Krasner working like a poet—with restraint while suggesting motion, painted strips of green and magenta allowing the background to say even more in negative space. Everything from her life—all the craft and technique, the suffering and the inspiration, the struggle and the sloughing off, the layers of knowledge and of love—all of it is here, in this work.

When he was credited with having trained the celebrity, Jackson Pollock, Krasner’s old teacher Hans Hofmann replied that Pollock was not his student—Pollock was the student of his student. How right he was.

“Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, on view October 4, 2026–January 31, 2027

items.title: Surveillance Pricers, Elizabeth Warren Is Coming for You
items.content_text:
The New York City Council on Thursday voted to ban surveillance pricing, joining Maryland, New Jersey, and Connecticut in doing so. Mayor Zohran Mamdani is expected to sign it. “New Yorkers’ personal data should never be used as a weapon against their own pocketbooks,” he said in a statement to local media. “Our administration will continue working with the council to protect workers, tenants, and consumers and put an end to the scam economy.”

Surveillance pricing is a practice many companies use to monitor customers and set prices digitally, sometimes charging customers more depending on where they are, how much they make, when they’re shopping, and other data gathered on them through their apps and loyalty programs. It is also something Democrats in Washington, D.C., are likely to aim for next year when they take over Congress. Whether they follow through on this issue will be a telling test of how broad they perceive their mandate to fight for the working class to be.

Arguing that populist economic policies drove the nationwide election results, Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren said at a progressive conference Tuesday that incoming Democrats should rein in the Trump family and corporate corruption through budget reconciliation or new legislation and dare President Trump to veto popular reforms, including bans on AI surveillance pricing. “We won big by naming what is wrong and convincing voters that we would take on a rigged system in order to fix it,” she said. “But here’s the thing. It would be a tremendous breach of faith with the people who voted for us to spend the next two years ahead of the 2028 election railing against Trump and waiting for a future Democratic trifecta to deliver meaningful change.”

Tackling surveillance pricing combines voter concerns over high pricing and the infiltration of artificial intelligence tools into more and more parts of their everyday life. “I think surveillance pricing sits nicely at the intersection of both overreach in Big Tech and overreach in Washington, but also higher prices,” said Lindsay Owens, president and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, which co-hosted the conference, Popular Mandate, with other progressive think tanks and organizations.

And while there’s the potential bipartisan support for banning surveillance pricing, Democrats can do a lot to show they’re on the side of working people just by taking on the issue, even if President Trump refuses to sign any legislation.

Part of the reason we know so much about the use of digital surveillance and algorithmic pricing and how much it costs families is that Groundwork has been investigating companies and publishing its findings. Primarily driven through apps, algorithmic pricing uses information gathered on consumers, posing privacy concerns and undermining transparency in pricing. A year ago, Groundwork released a report showing that Instacart, the grocery shopping app, charged customers wildly different prices in a pricing experiment. The average cost swings could add up to $1,200 per family per year, the report found. Instacart stopped its pricing tests after the report generated outrage.

Of course, it’s not just Instacart. Warren joined progressive representatives to demand answers on McDonald’s use of AI pricing, and the Federal Trade Commission targeted nine companies—Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target, and Walmart—in an investigation launched in October. In addition to costing customers more, regulators think algorithms might provide opportunities for collusion that violates antitrust rules. A 2023 antitrust lawsuit against Realpage, a real estate tool used by landlords to set rents, was just settled with $360 million awarded to the impacted renters. Many states are already working to ban such practices, and Missouri Senator Josh Hawley, a Republican, is among those who have called for federal legislation.

But investigations and hearings could accomplish a lot on their own. Democrats are reviewing plans from Groundwork to investigate corporations using their new platform as the majority party, which would give them opportunities to subpoena information and force CEOs to testify. It would also provide the opportunity for members to champion fixes to the cost and wage issues that Americans who live paycheck to paycheck care most about. Owens said the investigations themselves could prompt companies to stop these practices, pointing to the Instacart experience.

Of course, some more conservative members might balk at going after corporations too harshly, and centrist think tanks and consultants warn that being seen as broadly anti-business could backfire. But there’s evidence voters want these types of hearings. In a poll commissioned by Groundwork and performed by Hart Research during early voting and just after Election Day in Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas, voters listed “cares about and fights for working people and people like me” as the top reason for choosing their Democratic Senate candidate.

While prices and the cost of living were voters’ top concern, voters also believe the problem goes beyond inflation. “The economy has deeper problems than just high prices for everyday essentials. For too long, the system has favored the wealthy and large corporations at the expense of working families. Bringing down prices is important, but what we really need are fundamental changes so the economy works for everyone, not just those at the top” got support from 52 percent of all voters and 71 percent of Democratic voters, while a statement focusing just on prices and inflation got support from 44 percent of all voters and 26 percent of Democratic voters. Some of that is linked to practices like surveillance pricing, which seems unfair and unpredictable. How can a mom or dad budget for their family if they have no idea what their household’s food is going to cost from one week to the next?

Voters don’t think that the government moves too slowly to address issues like prices and corporate power. They think it hasn’t been a priority for their elected officials, and that’s what voters want changed. The statement “Government prioritizes the interests of billionaires, big corporations, and lobbyists instead of fighting for the interests of average Americans” got support from 62 percent of all voters and 84 percent of Democrats.

If Democrats launch a program to truly investigate the corporations relying on surveillance and algorithmic pricing, they could do something even more important than lower prices for consumers: They could show voters they’re on their side. That’s especially because many of the incoming senators and representatives are talented communicators, using social media tools and expertise to get their message straight to voters.

Communicating to constituents is an important part of an elected official’s job, and sharing YouTube clips and Instagram reels of members grilling CEOs about their pricing practices could be part of that. Anti–price gouging rules could be an easy win. But if hearings and a few easy wins are the only things Democrats accomplish, it won’t be enough to relieve the pain many working-class families feel. They need to be in for a long fight.

This article has been updated.

items.title: MAGA Propagandist Paid by Russian Government Shows Up at Mar-a-Lago
items.content_text:
Right-wing commentator Lauren Chen—who was a central figure in a 2024 indictment related to conservative influencers getting paid to spread “Russian government messaging”—just received a warm welcome at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago country club.

“First time at Mar-a-Lago,” Chen wrote on X, along with multiple fit pics of her at the Citizen Journalist Gala hosted by right-wing activist James O’Keefe at Mar-a-Lago on Thursday.

Chen, a Canadian influencer, founded Tenet Media with her husband in 2022, while she was also contributing to Turning Point USA. Two former RT employees were indicted two years later for giving Chen’s company a $10 million contract to inject pro-Russian propaganda into the conservative media landscape. Chen hired Dave Rubin, Tim Pool, and Benny Johnson, among others. The indictment noted that the influencers were paid to put out English-language videos that were “often consistent with Russia’s interest in amplifying U.S. domestic divisions in order to weaken U.S. opposition to core Russian interests.”

Shortly after news of the federal indictment, YouTube removed Tenet Media’s account, Chen was fired from her job with Blaze Media, and she fled the U.S. along with her husband.

“In case anyone has forgotten, Lauren fled the United States in 2024 after the DOJ exposed her for taking millions of dollars from sanctioned Russian entities to hire podcasters to push propaganda to conservatives,” The Scroll’s Park MacDougald wrote online. “She was publicly welcomed back into the United States last year by State Department employee [Joe Rittenhouse] and subsequently invited to the White House Easter Egg Roll. She is now at MAL.”

“Lauren Chen, financed by the Kremlin. ‘First time at Mar-a-Lago,’” journalist and former Polish Ambassador to the U.S. Marek Magierowski said. “It looks like creeping invasion. Congratulations to @SecretService.”

In any other administration, a woman who took money from the Russian government to influence U.S. media being welcomed at the president’s private estate would be a massive scandal. In year two of Trump’s second term, it is merely par for the course.

items.title: Mississippi GOP Leader Loses It as Experian Exposes Election Disaster
items.content_text:
Mississippi’s Senate race was marred by people being wrongly disqualified from the state voter rolls because of bad data, and the Republican secretary of state is having trouble taking responsibility.

Secretary of State Michael Watson’s office used data on expired addresses from the credit agency Experian to purge Mississippi’s voter rolls, even after being warned that the data was unreliable. On Thursday, Watson threatened to sue the credit agency in a deleted social media post, according to Democracy Docket, after Experian told The Atlantic earlier this week that its data shouldn’t have been used for voter records.

“The solution provided at that time consisted of supplemental address information and was not designed or intended to validate voter records,” Experian vice president for corporate communications Scott Anderson said.

In his now-deleted post, Watson claimed that the credit agency was “crawfishing away” from the state, tagging the Election Assistance Commission, an independent government agency that aids states with elections.

“Should we consider a lawsuit?” Watson wrote to the EAC. “They marketed a product for a specific reason and are now saying it wasn’t designed for that reason. More to come …”

Watson posted again the same day, attacking an article by Experian on its website saying that commercial data could be used to improve voter records.

“Since Experian doesn’t like the heat and appears as if they will not stand by their customers, they may want to delete the below piece from their website,” Watson wrote in a post that is still up.

In a statement to Democracy Docket, Watson’s communications director, Elizabeth Jonson, said that “Mississippi was never told the data was only supplemental or that it was not intended for this use.”

But Mississippi Today reported as early as March that Experian’s data was faulty, and a coalition of civil rights groups sent another last-minute warning to Watson’s office four days before the midterms asking him to reinstate people who were kicked off the voter rolls because of Experian’s data. Those warnings went unheeded, and the state’s election results dragged on because thousands of residents were forced to use affidavit ballots, which had to go through extra steps of verification before being counted.

items.title: Top Trump Adviser to Quit After Stinging Election Defeat
items.content_text:
Kevin Hassett, the smiling face of President Donald Trump’s disastrous economic policy, is expected to leave his role as director of the National Economic Council.

Hassett is expected to depart sometime in the next few weeks, three people familiar with his plans told Semafor Friday. Trump’s happy warrior has been eyeing different positions in the administration since well before the midterm elections, some people said.  

Affordability emerged as a major issue in the recent midterm elections, where Republican candidates suffered sweeping losses and Democrats flipped both the House and Senate. The economy has become one of Trump’s worst issues; a recent poll found that 67 percent of Americans disapproved of the president’s handling of the economy. 

As the mouthpiece for Trump’s crumbling economy, Hassett lied about lowering prices, denied data, and, of course, blamed everything on former President Joe Biden. And he did it all with a grin on his face. 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who could hold both jobs, and his counselor David Zervos are among those being considered to replace Hassett. This news comes amid renewed calls to remove Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, this time over his alleged efforts to shield Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese intelligence asset from scrutiny.

items.title: Donald Trump Cancels Second Mainstream Interview in Days
items.content_text:
Donald Trump pulled out of another mainstream interview Thursday–this time nixing a sit-down with NBC News.

The interview, CNN reported, would be in Philadelphia with NBC News' senior business correspondent, Christine Romans. CNN’s Brian Stelter said one source suggested that it had only been “postponed.”

It was the second time in a week that he had canceled a scheduled appearance outside the conservative news sphere, CNN’s Reliable Sources reported Thursday. He had canceled an in-studio appearance on the CNBC flagship show, Squawk Box, which was due on Friday.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Mitch McConnell Called Donald Trump a ‘Stupid’ and ‘Despicable Human Being’
items.content_text:
Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell called his party’s presidential nominee, Donald Trump, a “stupid,” “ill-tempered,” and “despicable human being,” according to his own records.

McConnell made the withering assessments in a series of private “personal oral histories” that he gave to Michael Tackett, the deputy Washington bureau chief of the Associated Press, who has a forthcoming biography about the Kentucky senator called The Price of Power. The AP conveniently reported the book’s juicy details.

McConnell’s remarks were made after the 2020 election that Trump lost, and the senator was apparently elated to see the backside of the former president, musing, “it’s not just the Democrats who are counting the days” until he leaves office.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Witnesses Say Would-Be Organ Donor Started ‘Thrashing’ on the Table
items.content_text:
Disaster was averted at a Kentucky hospital when an ostensibly deceased organ donor began “thrashing” around in the operating theater, a preservationist tells NPR.

“He was moving around,” Natasha Miller recalled of the patient, whom NPR identified as Anthony Thomas “TJ” Hoover II. “He was crying visibly.”

The two surgeons assigned to the transplant naturally refused to go through with the procedure, which was reportedly scheduled to take place at Baptist Health Richmond Hospital in October 2021. But when her colleague called Kentucky Organ Donor Affiliates, which coordinated the harvest, Miller said the supervisor told them they “were going to do the case” and needed to “find another doctor.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Menendez Family Members: We Had ‘Gut-Level’ Fears Erik and Lyle Were Sexually Abused
items.content_text:
Relatives of Lyle and Erik Menendez spoke in an interview Wednesday about their long-running fears that the brothers had been abused for years before they killed their parents.

After a press conference in which they’d called for the imprisoned siblings’ freedom, the family members told Chris Cuomo on NewsNation about how their suspicions only deepened as time passed.

“Over the years we really did know that there was abuse at gut-level. But as time goes on and we all talked to each other more and more, it validates the fears and the gut-level reactions that we had,” the brothers’ cousin Karen VanderMolen-Copley told Cuomo. “That solidified the knowledge that the sexual abuse actually did occur, because that’s not something you want to believe, and then once you talk to each other it becomes more and more obvious.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Liam Payne 911 Caller Said One Direction Star’s Life Could Be in Danger Minutes Before Death
items.content_text:
A hotel worker called 911 to request urgent assistance before musician Liam Payne fell to his death from the third floor of the building in Buenos Aires on Wednesday.

The 31-year-old British singer and former member of the boy band One Direction died after he “jumped from the balcony of his room,” Buenos Aires Security Ministry Communications Director Pablo Policicchio told the Associated Press. He added that police had been called to the Casa Sur Hotel in the Argentine capital after receiving an emergency call shortly after 5 p.m. local time about an “aggressive man who could be under the influence of drugs or alcohol.”

A transcript of a 911 call published by the BBC shows a worker at the hotel telling the operator that they have “a guest who is high on drugs and who is trashing the room” and the staff therefore “need someone to come.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Stormy Daniels Says Trump Is Trying to Silence Her Again
items.content_text:
It appears Donald Trump is once again attempting to silence Stormy Daniels, despite his recent convictions in that category.

MSNBC’s Rachel Maddow reports that Trump’s lawyers tried to “get another hush money deal” with the adult film star, to keep her from making any “public or private statements related to any alleged past interactions” with the former president. In exchange for her written agreement, Trump’s team reportedly offered to adjust the debt she owes Trump for the unsuccessful defamation case her lawyer brought against him in 2018.

Daniels still needs to pay “hundreds of thousands of dollars” in legal fees, Maddow explained, and in hammering out the exact amount, Trump’s lawyers allegedly offered to “pretend” she owed their client “less than they actually believed” she did. Whereas they first estimated Daniels’ debt at $650,000, Maddow reported, they said they would settle her tab for $620,000, if she promised not to make any “defamatory or disparaging statements about him, his business, and/or any affiliates, or his suitability as a candidate for president.” They then adjusted the fee, asking $635,000 if she refused to sign a non-disclosure agreement. Daniels reportedly turned them down, paying $627,500 and declining to sign the NDA.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Trump Calls Jan. 6, the Day His Supporters Led a Failed Insurrection, ‘A Day of Love’
items.content_text:
Former President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Jan. 6, 2021— the day his supporters occupied Congress in a failed insurrection to try to stop lawmakers from certifying Joe Biden’s election victory—was a “day of love.”

Trump made the baffling claim during a televised election town hall hosted by Univision.

Ramiro González, a construction worker from Tampa, told the meeting he deregistered as a Republican because he found Trump’s “inaction” during both Jan. 6 and the COVID-19 pandemic “disturbing.” He asked Trump to square his controversial behavior during the attack on the U.S. Capitol—and the fact that many of his own former administration officials don’t support him any longer—with why he should be re-elected.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Tegan and Sara: The Pop-Rock Twins Driven Mad by a Wild Catfishing Scheme
items.content_text:
Online interactions are based on trust, since there are few definitive ways to certify the identity of the person with whom one is communicating. Naturally, this situation can lead to deception and manipulation, as it has—to tormenting effect—for Tegan and Sara, the popular indie rock duo whose lives have been turned upside down by a mysterious bad faith actor who, for more than a decade, has impersonated Tegan with fans, friends, and business partners.

Fanatical: The Catfishing of Tegan and Sara is an investigation into the myriad means by which the internet can be wielded to nefarious ends. More than that, though, it’s an anatomy of a crime and the complicated wreckage wrought by it, not just for the famous artists but also for the innocent admirers who were tricked into believing that fiction was reality.

Premiering on Hulu on Oct. 18, following its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, Erin Lee Carr’s documentary is a chilling snapshot of the unholy marriage of corrosive fandom and online duplicity. At its center are Tegan and Sara, the identical twin songstresses who began making a name for themselves in the early 2000s both for their talent and for being openly gay. This earned them a loyal fanbase of queer women and men who saw themselves reflected in Tegan and Sara, and that bond was strengthened by the siblings’ active interest in interacting with fans in person—Tegan would chat with show attendees in line and at the merch table—and on LiveJournal and other budding message-board platforms that afforded a previously unavailable degree of contact.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: ‘Anora’: The Screwball Stripper Odyssey That Should Win All the Oscars
items.content_text:
Movies can’t, by definition, be all things to all people, and yet Anora—winner of the Cannes Film Festival’s highest honor, the Palme d’Or—manages to vacillate between assorted registers with stunning, and ultimately affecting, aplomb.

Another of The Florida Project and Red Rocket writer/director Sean Baker’s tales of marginalized individuals struggling to survive and find themselves in an often-unforgiving world, the film is a character study, romance, crime saga, screwball comedy, and vérité drama all wrapped into one unique and dexterous package. More impressive than its nimbleness, however, is its poise and empathy, the latter of which is chiefly bestowed upon its protagonist, whose life is thrown for a rollercoaster-grade loop-di-loop thanks to a chance introduction.

Ani (Mikey Madison, in a star-making turn) is a Brighton Beach 23-year-old who lives with her sister and earns a living stripping at a local club. Anora, which hits theaters Oct. 18, introduces her at the end of a long pan along a bench where men are receiving lap dances from erotic professionals. Fixating on Ani’s face as she flashes the fake smile that her customers crave and her superiors demand, Baker’s camera creates immediate, intimate engagement with the young woman, and that continues as it presents snapshots of her daily (or, rather, nightly) routine at her place of employment.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

items.title: Jimmy Kimmel Mocks Fox News’ Post-Harris Interview ‘Orgy’
items.content_text:
In his monologue Wednesday, Jimmy Kimmel played a montage of Fox News anchors praising Bret Baier for his interview with Kamala Harris, where they described Baier’s performance as “incredible” and “a masterful job.”

Kimmel responded, “Alright, save it for the post-show orgy, everybody! Come on now.”

The late night host was skeptical that the Fox News pundits’ praise came from a genuine place of journalistic integrity. “They all sit there in fear, imagining Donald Trump on the toilet watching them,” he said.
